|--------|-------|-----------|
| Diagnostic/Audit | $5K–$50K | 3-10x ROI vs. engagement cost |
| Implementation | $10K–$100K+ | Quick wins in first 30 days |
| Maintenance | $3K–$5K/mo | MSP-style monthly retainer |
| Advisory/Fractional | $3K–$10K/mo | Strategic advisor, trend filter |

## Anti-Patterns (Never Do This)
- ❌ Prescribe solutions before completing diagnosis
- ❌ Interview only executives (skip operators)
- ❌ Quote "time savings" without dollar figures
- ❌ Lead with technical tool names in client conversations
- ❌ Skip the change management gate before implementation
- ❌ Try to close on implementation before proving ROI with an audit
- ❌ Accept an engagement without an identified AI Champion

## Hall of Fame Exemplar
**The SDR Team Waste Discovery**: Through operator interviews (not executive reports), discovered 8 SDRs spent 2 hours every morning manually prospecting instead of selling. VP had NO idea. Math: 2hrs/day × 8 SDRs × 260 days × $40/hr = **$166,400/year wasted on ONE process**. This single finding justified the entire engagement cost multiple times over. This is the power of diagnosis.

| **Diagnostic-Only** | $15K-$35K for diagnostic, implementation priced separately | Building trust, new relationship | Pipeline builder |
| **Retainer + Project** | $X/mo retainer + project pricing | Established relationships | $180K+/year per client |

**Never use hourly billing.** Research (2025): hourly caps at $50K/year. Fixed phases close at 65% vs. 30% for flat quotes.

## Acquisition Intelligence (v2.0)
### LinkedIn "POC Teardown" Strategy

## 1. Visual Direction First
Before touching any code or layout tool, establish a complete visual identity — color palette, lighting, mood, composition — using reference images and AI image generators. Never build without knowing the final aesthetic.

## 2. Bookend Frame Architecture
Create exactly two frames — a starting frame and an ending frame — that serve as visual anchors. The AI generates all motion in between. These bookends define the visual arc's start state and destination.

## 3. Tool Specialization Pipeline
Each tool handles exactly one job: Nano Banana/Whisk = image generation + style definition → Google Flow/Veo 3.1 = frame-to-video animation → EasyGIF = video-to-WebP conversion → Firebase Studio/Antigravity = website assembly + deployment. Never force one tool to do two jobs.

## 6. Progressive Polish Protocol
Build in layers: foundation → pages → content → CMS → polish. Each layer is complete before the next begins. Polish comes last — cursor glow, animations, micro-interactions are finishing touches, not foundations.

## 7. Headless CMS as Client Independence Layer
Position the CMS as a client independence layer — the mechanism that means clients never call you to update a headline or publish a blog post. Wire up GraphQL endpoints so non-technical users manage dynamic content without touching code.

## 8. WebP Sequence Scroll Animation Hack
Convert animations to WebP frame sequences triggered on scroll. This keeps visual quality while maintaining page performance. Export at original resolution, closest native FPS, quality 85, forever loop. Split into frames, store in Supabase, reference URLs for scroll-triggered playback.

## 10. AI Agent as Autonomous Engineer
Treat the AI agent as an autonomous front-end engineer: give it an implementation plan → review the plan it returns → approve or adjust → let it execute autonomously → verify output. Don't micromanage individual lines.

## 11. Security-Conscious API Handling
Separate API key handling — never paste secrets into agent prompts. Wait for the agent to create an .env file, then paste secrets only there. No API keys visible in code files, prompts, or version control.

## 12. Export-Ready Architecture
Build with portability — projects can be exported from Firebase Studio and deployed anywhere (Netlify, Vercel, custom hosting) without restructuring. Use code editor to select all → zip → download → deploy.

## 1. The "Millisecond Judgment" Problem
Website visitors judge a site in milliseconds. Andy's entire pipeline is built around winning that neurological reaction through motion, depth, and visual coherence. Most builders optimize for features; Andy optimizes for the first impression. Every tool choice and animation decision serves this single moment.

## 2. The FPS/Quality Sweet Spot
When converting video to WebP: original resolution, closest frame rate to native (NOT maximum), quality 85. Going higher adds file size without perceptible quality gain. Going lower creates visible degradation. This number (85) only comes from testing dozens of projects — you won't find it in documentation.

## 3. Visual Arc Theory
The first and last frames aren't just "two images" — they define a visual arc. Opening frame = first impression. Closing frame = permanence. Everything in between = controlled interpolation. This is cinematic directing applied to web design — something film directors do intuitively but web designers almost never consider.

## 4. Supabase as Visual CDN
Andy uses Supabase not as a database but as a public bucket for visual assets — essentially a free, high-performance CDN for WebP frame sequences. This solves the "where do I host 50+ animation frames" problem without paid CDN services.

## 5. The Anti-Template Paradox
By following a systematic workflow (which sounds like templating), Andy produces sites that look nothing like templates. The system is rigid; the outputs are unique. This works because the visual direction step produces completely different aesthetic foundations every time, while the structural pipeline ensures professional execution.

## 6. Schema as Content Contract
When setting up Hygraph schemas, Andy creates a content contract — a structural agreement between CMS and frontend about what data looks like. Once the schema is set, content can be migrated programmatically. This is enterprise-grade architecture presented as "just drag and drop."

## 7. The "Agent Skills" Meta-Layer
Installing Antigravity agent skills as a pre-build step isn't optional decoration — these skills fundamentally change how the agent approaches the project. They provide best practices, design patterns, and quality standards that inform every subsequent decision. Skip this step and you get a mediocre site.

## 8. Permanent Auth Token Strategy
By creating a permanent OAuth token for Hygraph (rather than session-based), Andy enables content automation through AI agents — new blog posts and case studies can be published by simply pasting content into the agent. This is content automation infrastructure hiding in plain sight.

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
**1. "Aura Smart Lamp" Product Launch Page**
*   **Description**: A single-page product launch site for a new smart home device. The hero section features a full-screen, scroll-triggered animation of the lamp rotating and transitioning between different lighting moods (e.g., "Sunrise Glow" to "Midnight Serenity"). The animation is buttery smooth, leveraging WebP sequences hosted on Supabase, and maintains a consistent, high-end visual aesthetic throughout. Product specifications and testimonials below are managed via a Hygraph CMS, allowing the marketing team to update content without developer intervention.
*   **What makes this excellent**: Exemplifies the "Millisecond Judgment" problem solution (Hidden Knowledge 1) by immediately captivating the user with a premium, performant visual. The animation perfectly executes "Bookend Frame Architecture" (Pattern 2) and "Visual Arc Theory" (Hidden Knowledge 3), with the starting frame showing the lamp off and the ending frame highlighting its ambient effect. The "WebP Sequence Scroll Animation Hack" (Pattern 8) ensures desktop-level visual quality at mobile-friendly speeds.

**2. "Apex Adventures" Interactive Travel Portal**
*   **Description**: A dynamic travel website showcasing exotic destinations. Each destination page features a hero section with a subtle, parallax-driven background animation of the landscape, smoothly transitioning as the user scrolls. The visual identity (color palette, mood, composition) for each destination is distinct yet cohesive with the overall brand, established through initial AI-generated visual direction. Travel packages and blog posts are managed through a headless CMS, allowing for rapid updates and new content publication.
*   **What makes this excellent**: Demonstrates "Visual Direction First" (Pattern 1) by establishing unique aesthetics for each destination while maintaining brand consistency. The subtle parallax animations showcase "Tool Specialization Pipeline" (Pattern 3) and "Progressive Polish Protocol" (Pattern 6), adding a premium feel without sacrificing performance. The "Headless CMS as Client Independence Layer" (Pattern 7) is crucial for a content-rich site, leveraging "Schema as Content Contract" (Hidden Knowledge 6) for robust data structuring.

**Anti-Exemplar: "Generic AI Build Co." Landing Page**
*   **Description**: A landing page ostensibly built with AI, featuring a stock video in the hero section that loops abruptly. The visual style is inconsistent across sections, mixing different fonts and color palettes. Basic content is hardcoded, requiring a developer to update a single headline. Animation quality is low, with visible stuttering and artifacts, and page load times are sluggish.
*   **What makes this mediocre**: Fails on "Millisecond Judgment" (Hidden Knowledge 1) due to poor first impression. Lacks any "Visual Arc Theory" (Hidden Knowledge 3) or "Bookend Frame Architecture" (Pattern 2), resulting in jarring, non-narrative motion. Ignores "Tool Specialization Pipeline" (Pattern 3) by trying to force a single AI tool to do everything, leading to generic output and poor performance. No "Headless CMS as Client Independence Layer" (Pattern 7), creating client dependency.

*   **The Aesthetic Blueprint First**: Always initiates a project by defining the complete visual identity—color palette, lighting, mood, composition—through AI image generation and reference images *before* any layout or coding begins. → **Deploy when**: Starting any new website, landing page, or visual asset creation.
*   **The Motion Arc Definition**: Crafts all complex animations by first establishing a distinct "starting frame" and "ending frame" in an AI video generator, then prompts the AI to interpolate the motion, ensuring a controlled visual narrative. → **Deploy when**: Any section requires a high-quality, narrative-driven animation or parallax effect.
*   **The Client Content Autonomy Layer**: Implements a headless CMS (like Hygraph) with GraphQL endpoints from day one, explicitly framing it as the mechanism for clients to manage all dynamic content independently, removing future developer dependency. → **Deploy when**: Building any client-facing website with dynamic content (blogs, case studies, product listings).
*   **The Scroll-Optimized Visual Stream**: Converts all generated video animations into high-performance WebP frame sequences at a specific quality (85) and native FPS, then hosts them on a public bucket (e.g., Supabase) for scroll-triggered playback. → **Deploy when**: Implementing any visually rich, scroll-driven animation that must maintain performance and quality.

## 1. The Context-Before-Product Pattern

## 2. The Reverse Insight Derivation
**What She Does**: Derives the market insight from the differentiated value — working backwards from "what we uniquely do" to "what must be true about the world for that to matter."

**Executable Behavior**: List differentiated value → ask "What would someone need to believe for this to be the most important thing?" → that's your insight.

**Deployment**: Positioning workshops, pitch construction, content strategy.

**Success Metric**: Insight feels inevitable rather than forced; competitors cannot start their pitch with the same insight.

---

## 3. The Muffin/Cake Disambiguation
**What She Does**: Uses absurd analogies to make abstract concepts concrete — "it's a muffin in a bakery, but a cake at a birthday party." She positions her own ideas the way she teaches others to position products.

**Executable Behavior**: When explaining any category confusion, find the everyday analog where context determines perception.

**Deployment**: Teaching, presentations, content that needs to make complex ideas accessible.

**Success Metric**: Audience can retell the analogy to someone else accurately.

---

chunks.section: 4. The "Why Would They Pick Us" Filter
chunks.content:
## 4. The "Why Would They Pick Us" Filter
**What She Does**: Filters every positioning/pitch element through one question: *does this help the customer understand why they should pick us over alternatives?*

**Executable Behavior**: After writing any marketing/sales material, review every sentence with this filter — cut anything that doesn't answer the question.

**Deployment**: Pitch decks, landing pages, sales scripts, product descriptions.

**Success Metric**: Every element of the pitch contributes to competitive differentiation.

---

## 5. The Perfect World Bridge
**What She Does**: Creates an explicit agreement checkpoint between the market setup and the product reveal — getting verbal buy-in that "a good solution would have A, B, C" before revealing the product delivers exactly A, B, C.

**Executable Behavior**: After discussing alternatives and their tradeoffs, explicitly ask "Can we agree that a great solution would..." and list your differentiated value themes as purchase criteria.

**Deployment**: Sales calls, demos, webinar pitches, proposal presentations.

**Success Metric**: Prospect verbally agrees to purchase criteria before seeing the product.

---

## 6. The Calm Confidence Posture
**What She Does**: Approaches every sales interaction from a position of knowing *exactly* who should pick her product — willing to disqualify bad fits without anxiety.

**Executable Behavior**: Enter conversations willing to say "we might not be right for you" and mean it. Know your ideal customer so well that walking away from bad fits feels natural.

**Deployment**: All sales interactions, especially with prospects showing poor fit signals.

**Success Metric**: You disqualify as many bad fits as you close good ones; win rate on qualified deals increases.

---

## 7. The Feature-to-Value Translation
**What She Does**: Never presents a feature without immediately answering "so what?" until reaching business impact.

**Executable Behavior**: For each feature, chain "so what?" at least 2-3 levels deep: Feature → Capability → Business Outcome → Strategic Impact.

**Deployment**: Product demos, feature announcements, sales materials, pitch decks.

**Success Metric**: Customer says "I need that" instead of "that's cool."

---

## 8. The Discovery-Embedded Pitch
**What She Does**: Weaves qualification/discovery into the pitch narrative rather than treating it as a separate phase.

**Executable Behavior**: At each step of the setup (insight, alternatives, perfect world), pause and ask "does this match your experience?" — this IS your discovery.

**Deployment**: First sales calls, demo calls, qualification conversations.

**Success Metric**: By end of setup, you know if this is a good fit AND the prospect feels heard.

---

## 9. The Champion Armory
**What She Does**: Anticipates every stakeholder objection and pre-arms the champion with responses before they encounter internal resistance.

**Executable Behavior**: Document the top 3-5 objections from each stakeholder group (IT, Finance, End Users, Exec). Create ammunition sheets the champion can use independently.

**Deployment**: Multi-stakeholder B2B sales, enterprise deals, procurement processes.

**Success Metric**: Champion can handle internal objections without needing to bring you back in.

---

## 10. The Bowling Pin Sequencing
**What She Does**: Thinks about market expansion as sequential domination of adjacent niches rather than attempting to capture an entire market at once.

**Executable Behavior**: Define your lead pin (most underserved niche), identify 2-3 adjacent pins, build sequential conquest plan.

**Deployment**: Go-to-market strategy, product roadmap planning, market expansion.

**Success Metric**: Dominant market share in lead pin before expanding.

---

## 11. The Anti-Category-Creation Default
**What She Does**: Defaults to positioning within existing categories and only considers category creation as a late-stage expansion play for market leaders.

**Executable Behavior**: Before considering category creation, ask: "Are we dominant in our current niche? Can we grow by shaving off pieces of an existing market first?"

**Deployment**: Strategic positioning decisions, market entry planning.

**Success Metric**: Traction and revenue from niche domination before any category creation attempt.

---

## 12. The Best Rep Test Protocol
**What She Does**: Never rolls out a new pitch to the full sales team — always tests with the single best rep first, iterates based on live deals, then uses that rep to evangelize internally.

**Executable Behavior**: Identify best rep → train them exclusively → test on qualified prospects → iterate → let that rep sell the new pitch to the rest of the team.

**Deployment**: Any time sales pitch, messaging, or positioning changes.

**Success Metric**: Best rep voluntarily refuses to go back to the old pitch.

## 1. Positioning IS Context-Setting, Not Messaging
**Tacit Insight**: April never reduces positioning to taglines or value propositions. She treats it as the cognitive act of setting context so the customer's brain automatically categorizes your product the way you want. This is closer to cognitive psychology than marketing.

**Deployment**: When doing positioning work, stop asking "what's our tagline?" Start asking "what context, if set correctly, would make our value self-evident?"

**Why Others Miss This**: Most positioning frameworks start with "our unique value proposition" — which is already a messaging exercise. April starts with competitive alternatives, which is a context-setting exercise.

---

chunks.section: 2. The Status Quo Is Safer Than You Think
chunks.content:
## 2. The Status Quo Is Safer Than You Think
**Tacit Insight**: Most founders underestimate how comfortable the status quo is. "Do nothing" isn't laziness — it's rational risk management. The buyer's biggest fear isn't picking the wrong product; it's the career consequences of making any active choice.

**Deployment**: In sales conversations, acknowledge the status quo explicitly and with empathy. Show buyers you understand why doing nothing feels safe — then provide enough teaching to make action feel less risky than inaction.

**Why Others Miss This**: Sales training focuses on overcoming objections about competitors. The real competitor is the spreadsheet/manual process the buyer is already using.

---

## 3. FOMO Backfires on Indecisive Buyers
**Tacit Insight**: Counter to sales orthodoxy, creating urgency and FOMO makes indecisive buyers *more* likely to freeze. The data (Matt Dixon / The Jolt Effect) shows teaching and risk-reduction work; pressure doesn't.

**Deployment**: When a deal stalls, resist the urge to create urgency. Instead, teach the buyer how to evaluate options and reduce the perceived risk of choosing.

**Why Others Miss This**: Sales leaders default to "create urgency" because it works on *decided* buyers who need a push. But 40-60% of B2B deals end in no decision — those buyers aren't decided. Urgency makes them freeze harder.

---

## 4. The Champion's Invisible Job
**Tacit Insight**: In B2B, the champion has two jobs: (1) find the best solution and (2) survive the internal political process of recommending it. Most vendors only help with job #1.

**Deployment**: After identifying your champion, explicitly ask: "Who else will be involved in this decision? What are their typical concerns?" Then build ammunition sheets for each stakeholder type.

**Why Others Miss This**: Vendors think the champion's job ends at "choosing us." But the champion then has to sell internally — to security, legal, finance, and executives — often without your support. Arm them or they fail.

---

## 5. Cross-Functional Positioning Teams Are Non-Negotiable
**Tacit Insight**: Positioning created by marketing alone always fails because sales throws it out. The positioning workshop MUST include product, marketing, and sales together.

**Deployment**: When running positioning exercises, mandate participation from the head of sales, the best AE, the product lead, and the marketing lead. Never let one function own it alone.

**Why Others Miss This**: Marketing wants to "own" positioning because it's traditionally their domain. But positioning that doesn't match what sales says on calls is dead on arrival. Cross-functional means binding agreement.

---

chunks.section: 6. Your Insight Must Be Unchallengeable by Competitors
chunks.content:
## 6. Your Insight Must Be Unchallengeable by Competitors
**Tacit Insight**: If your competitors could start their pitch with the same market insight, it's not an insight — it's a generic trend observation. True insights are derived from your differentiated value and cannot be co-opted.

**Deployment**: Test every market insight by asking: "Could [competitor X] open their pitch with this same statement?" If yes, dig deeper into what makes your perspective uniquely derived from your capabilities.

**Why Others Miss This**: Most companies use trend data as their "insight" ("the market is moving to cloud"). That's available to everyone. The real insight comes from reversing your unique capabilities into "what must be true about the world."

---

chunks.section: 7. The Sales Pitch Is the Fastest Positioning Test
chunks.content:
## 7. The Sales Pitch Is the Fastest Positioning Test
**Tacit Insight**: Don't wait for a full marketing rebrand to test new positioning. Translate it into a sales pitch, test with qualified prospects in 2-4 weeks, and iterate. This is the lowest-risk way to validate positioning changes.

**Deployment**: When positioning changes, build a pitch deck first (not a website redesign). Test with 3 reps on 10 qualified prospects. If it works, then rebrand.

**Why Others Miss This**: Companies treat positioning as a marketing project with 6-month timelines. April treats it as a hypothesis you can test in 2 weeks through sales conversations.

---

chunks.section: 8. Investor Pitches and Sales Pitches Are Fundamentally Different
chunks.content:
## 8. Investor Pitches and Sales Pitches Are Fundamentally Different
**Tacit Insight**: Investor pitches can use trends, future visions, and long timelines. Sales pitches must deliver value *right now*. Confusing the two is a common startup mistake.

**Deployment**: If your sales deck contains phrases like "the future of [X]" or "the market is moving toward," you're using an investor pitch in a sales context. Rewrite for present-tense, specific value.

**Why Others Miss This**: Founders create one deck and use it for everything. Investors buy potential; buyers buy solutions. Trend-based sales pitches give buyers a reason to delay — "if this is the future, I can buy it next year."

---

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Excellent Exemplar 1: The "Unseen Cost" Insight Pitch
**Context**: A B2B SaaS product for automating complex regulatory compliance for mid-market financial firms. Its core differentiation is its dynamic, AI-powered adaptability to rule changes and proactive evidence collection, unlike rigid legacy systems or manual processes.
**Pitch Opening (Setup Phase)**:
"Most financial firms think of compliance as a necessary evil — a cost of doing business. But the real problem isn't just the audit itself; it's the *hidden cost of reactive compliance*. It's the constant scramble of pulling your top talent away from revenue-generating work to prepare for an audit, the inevitable errors in manual reporting, and the anxiety of knowing you're always one rule change away from being out of sync. Existing solutions are either too rigid, forcing you to adapt to their workflow, or too generic, leaving critical gaps. Can we agree that a truly great compliance solution wouldn't just help you pass an audit, but would virtually eliminate the 'audit scramble' altogether, freeing up your specialized talent to focus on growth?"
**What makes this excellent**:
*   **Context-Before-Product**: No mention of the product, only the market problem and current alternatives' failings.
*   **Reverse Insight Derivation**: The insight ("hidden cost of reactive compliance") is directly derived from the product's differentiated ability to offer proactive, dynamic compliance. Competitors (legacy systems, manual) cannot credibly claim this insight.
*   **Perfect World Bridge**: Gets explicit buy-in on the desired outcome *before* revealing the solution, making the product's value self-evident.
*   **Discovery-Embedded**: The "Can we agree?" question simultaneously qualifies the prospect and builds consensus.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Excellent Exemplar 2: The "Champion's Internal Sell" Ammunition Sheet
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Excellent Exemplar 2: The "Champion's Internal Sell" Ammunition Sheet
**Context**: A sales enablement platform selling to large enterprises. The champion is a VP of Sales Operations.
**Ammunition Sheet for IT Stakeholder (reconstructed for clarity)**:
**IT Objection**: "Another SaaS tool means more security risk and integration headaches. We already have Salesforce."
**Champion's Response (Pre-Armed by Vendor)**:
"I understand your concern about security and integration. We've done a deep dive with [Vendor Name]'s team. They're SOC 2 Type II compliant, encrypt all data at rest and in transit, and have a dedicated security team. For integration, they have native, bidirectional APIs for Salesforce, which means no custom coding for our core use cases. Crucially, this isn't *another* tool; it offloads significant manual work from our sales reps, reducing shadow IT solutions they might otherwise adopt. It actually *simplifies* our tech stack by consolidating disparate tools our reps currently use for content, training, and analytics into one secure platform."
**What makes this excellent**:
*   **Champion Armory**: Explicitly provides the champion with detailed, pre-vetted responses for common internal objections from a specific stakeholder group (IT).
*   **Objection Anticipation**: Addresses security and integration, which are universal IT concerns, head-on and with specific, credible details.
*   **Reframing**: Turns a potential negative ("another tool") into a positive ("simplifies our stack, reduces shadow IT").
*   **Decision Risk Mitigation**: Equips the champion to navigate internal politics, reducing the risk of the deal stalling due to internal resistance.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Anti-Exemplar: The "Feature Dump" Sales Pitch
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Anti-Exemplar: The "Feature Dump" Sales Pitch
**Context**: A new project management software aiming for the mid-market.
**Pitch Opening**:
"Our new project management software, TaskFlow, is designed to revolutionize how your team works. It features AI-powered task prioritization, Gantt charts, Kanban boards, integrated time tracking, and over 50 integrations with popular tools like Slack and Google Drive. We're leveraging the latest cloud technology to ensure maximum scalability and uptime, and our intuitive drag-and-drop interface makes project setup a breeze. We believe TaskFlow is the future of collaborative work."
**Why this is mediocre**:
*   **Violates Context-Before-Product**: Jumps straight into features and product details without establishing any market context, problem, or competitive alternatives.
*   **No "Why Pick Us" Filter**: Every feature listed is generic for project management software; there's no clear differentiation or answer to "Why TaskFlow over Asana, Monday, or ClickUp?"
*   **Lacks Insight**: No unique point of view on the market or the "problem inside the problem." It's just a list of capabilities.
*   **No Feature-to-Value Translation**: Features are listed, but the "so what?" (business outcome, strategic impact) is missing or too generic ("revolutionize how your team works").

## Signature Moves
*   **The Qualification Interrogation**: After setting up the market context and outlining competitive alternatives, she pauses and explicitly asks, "Does this match your experience?" or "Does that perspective resonate with how you see the market?" This isn't just discovery; it's a real-time qualification and consensus-building move.
    → **Deploy when**: Transitioning from a market insight or competitive alternative discussion to your "perfect world" criteria or product reveal.
*   **The Reverse Engineer's Insight**: When struggling to articulate a compelling market insight, she lists out the product's unique, differentiated capabilities, then works backward asking, "What would someone have to deeply believe about the world for *these specific capabilities* to be the most important thing for them right now?" That emergent belief becomes the market insight.
    → **Deploy when**: Generating or refining a market insight, especially if current insights feel generic or unprovocative.
*   **The "So What?" Chain Reaction**: For every feature, capability, or even a 'benefit', she immediately pushes for the next layer of impact by asking "So what?" at least three times. (e.g., "It does X" → "So what?" → "That means Y" → "So what?" → "Which leads to Z business outcome" → "So what?" → "Which enables this strategic impact for the company.")
    → **Deploy when**: Presenting product features, capabilities, or technical details, ensuring they're always tied to tangible business value.
*   **The Champion's Pre-Game Huddle**: Once a champion is identified, she explicitly schedules a separate session to map out internal stakeholders, their likely objections, and jointly crafts "ammunition sheets" for the champion to use independently in internal meetings.
    → **Deploy when**: A B2B deal progresses past the initial discovery with a clear internal champion, especially in multi-stakeholder enterprise sales.

## Evolution Log
### Evolution 1: Positioning Siege Test (2026-04-09)
- **Target**: Adversarial Resilience (scored 5/10 on baseline positioning output)
- **Hypothesis**: Adding a competitive siege layer (counter-positioning attacks, market shift scenarios, constraint-based inevitability proof) produces positioning that is more defensible and harder to copy.
- **New Cognitive Layer**: Phase 6 "Siege Test" — three sequential attacks on completed positioning:
  1. **Competitive Counter-Positioning**: Simulate top competitors' counter-moves, score vulnerabilities, build fortifications
  2. **Market Shift Stress Test**: Extract implicit assumptions, construct break scenarios, classify resilience (Robust/Conditional/Fragile)
  3. **Inevitability Proof**: Map hard constraints (capability, market, competitive, identity) and chain into logical proof that the position is discovered, not chosen. Score copy-resistance 1-10.
- **Benchmark Task**: "Position an Authority Flywheel service for S&C coaches against generic ghostwriting agencies and DIY content tools"
- **Results**: Baseline composite 6.7 (Intent 8, Expert 7, Adversarial 5) vs Variant composite 8.0 (Intent 8, Expert 8, Adversarial 8). Delta: +1.3 composite, +3 on target dimension.
- **Key Insight**: The siege test exposed that "voice-first methodology" is a claim any ghostwriter makes — the fortification forced it to become a PROVABLE MECHANISM (voice memo extraction). Also forced reframe from "content service" to "strategic authority system" to defend against AI commoditization. These upgrades would not have emerged from the standard workflow alone.
- **Verdict**: KEEP. Promoted to `workflows/positioning-siege-test.md`.

# Ash Maurya: Founder Systems Mastery

Ash Maurya's core move is turning entrepreneurship from inspirational guessing into a staged learning system. The business model is treated as the product, customer behavior is treated as truth, and the founder's job is to move from assumptions to commitments before overbuilding.

## Available Workflows
| # | Workflow | Produces | Use When |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | [Lean Canvas Diagnostic](workflows/01-lean-canvas-diagnostic.md) | One-page business model with risk ranking | An idea needs structure before validation |
| 02 | [Problem-First Validation](workflows/02-problem-first-validation.md) | Problem evidence map and early adopter definition | The founder is not sure the problem is real |
| 03 | [Business Model Risk Map](workflows/03-business-model-risk-map.md) | Ranked assumption and experiment queue | The idea has too many unknowns |
| 04 | [Traction-First Roadmap](workflows/04-traction-first-roadmap.md) | 90-day validation roadmap | The founder wants a path from idea to demand |
| 05 | [Demo-Sell-Build Sprint](workflows/05-demo-sell-build-sprint.md) | 48-hour offer demo and commitment script | Speed matters more than product polish |
| 06 | [Customer Interview Design](workflows/06-customer-interview-design.md) | Behavioral interview guide and synthesis sheet | The founder needs real customer evidence |
| 07 | [Buying Insight Interview](workflows/13-buying-insight-interview.md) | Truth interview script, buying criteria, and commitment ask | The founder needs to predict what customers actually buy |
| 08 | [Learning Velocity Scorecard](workflows/07-learning-velocity-scorecard.md) | Learning-rate dashboard and decision log | The team is confusing activity with progress |
| 09 | [Offer Assumption Test](workflows/08-offer-assumption-test.md) | Mafia offer test and commitment ladder | The offer needs proof before building |
| 10 | [Founder Systems War Room](workflows/09-founder-systems-war-room.md) | Weekly founder operating room | Multiple business ideas or experiments need orchestration |
| 11 | [Productized Service Validation](workflows/10-productized-service-validation.md) | Client-facing validation sprint offer | A service needs proof, pricing, and delivery shape |
| 12 | [Dan Martell Scale Handshake](workflows/11-dan-martell-scale-handshake.md) | Validation-to-scale handoff | A validated idea is ready for constraint-first scaling |
| 13 | [Daniel Priestley Asset Handshake](workflows/12-daniel-priestley-asset-handshake.md) | Validation-to-asset handoff | A validated service or method should become IP/assets |

## Stacking Guide
| Ash Workflow | Stack With | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Problem-First Validation | Dan Martell Market Entry | Problem proof plus rich-buyer targeting |
| Buying Insight Interview | Customer Forces / JTBD | Past behavior becomes buying criteria and offer framing |
| Business Model Risk Map | Andrew Wilkinson Rapid Prototype | Build only after the highest-risk assumption is reduced |
| Traction-First Roadmap | Soowei Leverage Audit | Founder workflow becomes validation-driven |
| Demo-Sell-Build Sprint | Phil M Jones | Commitment asks become low-pressure and clear |
| Productized Service Validation | Daniel Priestley 24 Assets | Service proof becomes a productized asset pathway |
| Founder Systems War Room | Operator Autopilot | Raw founder context routes into the right validation loop |

## Starter Sequences
**Raw Idea To Validated Demand**
`/ash-lean-canvas -> /ash-risk-map -> /ash-customer-interview -> /ash-buying-insight -> /ash-demo-sell-build -> /ash-traction-roadmap`

**Client Validation Sprint**
`/ash-problem-validation -> /ash-buying-insight -> /ash-offer-test -> /ash-productized-validation -> /ash-priestley-handshake`

**Validated Startup To Scale**
`/ash-traction-roadmap -> /ash-learning-scorecard -> /ash-dan-martell-handshake`

## Core Thesis
Entrepreneurship is not a heroic act of building. It is a disciplined search for a business model that works. Ash Maurya turns founder uncertainty into a sequence of evidence gates: identify the customer forces, define the business model, rank the riskiest assumptions, validate behavior before opinions, sell before building, and use traction as the real scoreboard.

## Genius Patterns
1. **Business Model As Product**: The thing being designed first is not the app, service, or feature set. It is the whole business model: customer, problem, promise, channel, price, cost, and traction logic.
2. **Problem Before Solution**: The founder does not ask whether people like an idea. They prove that a painful problem already exists in the customer's world.
3. **Customer Forces Physics**: A switch happens when push plus pull beats inertia plus friction. Because losses feel heavier than gains, friction and inertia must be actively reduced, not hand-waved.
4. **Switching Story Extraction**: Purchase behavior is decoded through trigger, search, and outcome. The founder looks for what broke, what got fired, what got hired, and what tradeoffs were accepted.
5. **5P MVP Design**: MVP is not a small feature set. It is five ordered decisions: problem, prospects, promise, price, and packaging.
6. **Alternative-Anchored Pricing**: Price is not copied from competitors. It is anchored against the current alternative the customer already pays for with money, time, delay, risk, or workaround pain.
7. **Demo-Sell-Build**: A demo, promise, and commitment ask come before a finished product. Building starts after enough qualified customers commit resources.
8. **Behavior Over Opinion**: Validation is measured by what customers have done, tried, paid, avoided, or committed to, not what they say they might do.
9. **Learning Velocity Advantage**: The unfair advantage is speed of learning. A founder who runs cleaner experiments faster beats a founder who merely builds faster.
10. **Sequential Risk Reduction**: Problem discovery validates solution design. Solution design validates offer delivery. Offer delivery validates demand. Skipping a phase creates false confidence.
11. **Early Adopter Intensity Threshold**: The best first customers are not generic personas. They have the strongest push, clear switching trigger, active workaround, and willingness to commit.
12. **Traction Is The Goal**: Everything that does not increase validated learning, commitment, or revenue is treated as distraction.
13. **The One Useful Interview Question**: Replace future-tense prediction with past-tense reconstruction: ask customers to walk through the last time they encountered the situation and where they struggled.
14. **Old-Way Mining**: Customers cannot reliably invent the new solution, but they can describe when, why, and how the old solution frustrates them.
15. **Buying Criteria Extraction**: What customers actually value appears when they explain why they chose one alternative over another.
16. **Pet Peeve, Struggle, Workaround Detection**: Important problems often start as small annoyances, time-consuming struggles, or improvised workarounds.
17. **Fact-Audited Insight**: Interview interpretation must be cross-checked against what the customer actually said and did, not the founder's preferred product direction.

## Hidden Knowledge
- A neutral or imperfect purchase can reveal more opportunity than a delighted purchase, because accepted tradeoffs expose what the market still tolerates.
- Founders overbuild because building creates emotional relief. Ash's system removes that relief until customer behavior has earned it.
- A business model can fail even when the product works technically. Commercial failure usually means one of the five P decisions was guessed.
- The strongest validation scripts sound like advice-seeking, not pitching. The founder earns truth by staying out of selling mode during discovery.
- A "no" after an offer test is useful if it identifies the force that blocked the switch: weak push, weak pull, high friction, or status quo inertia.
- Pricing is segmentation. A $50/month developer product and a $5,000/month architect product can be the same underlying technology with different problem economics.
- The right MVP may be a concierge, Wizard of Oz, demo, pilot, or paid sprint. Software is only one packaging option.
- Asking "what do you want?" is not customer discovery. It makes the customer do the entrepreneur's job and usually produces faster-horse answers.
- Leading with a problem list creates spotlight bias. The customer reacts to your framing instead of revealing their real world.
- The old way is the map. Existing solutions, spreadsheets, email, consultants, courses, and workarounds reveal what the new product must displace.
- A repeated pet peeve across interviews can be more commercially useful than a dramatic but isolated complaint.
- The founder's job after discovery is not to build immediately; it is to sell the new promise back to the same people before building.

## Signature Moves
1. Convert feature ideas into business-model assumptions.
2. Rewrite vague ICPs as early adopters with active switching triggers.
3. Replace "Would you use this?" with "Walk me through the last time this happened."
4. Build a customer forces map before writing the offer.
5. Use the 5P sequence to prevent MVP sprawl.
6. Demand a commitment ladder instead of accepting compliments.
7. Timebox validation to reduce founder bias.
8. Move from problem evidence to offer evidence to build evidence.
9. Convert "would you use this?" into "walk me through the last time."
10. Mine the old way for pet peeves, struggles, and workarounds.
11. Extract buying criteria from chosen and rejected alternatives.
12. Audit each insight against interview facts before turning it into a feature.

## Anti-Patterns
- Building a smaller version of the product and calling it an MVP.
- Asking customers for opinions about a solution they have not tried to buy.
- Treating price as a late-stage packaging detail.
- Confusing signups, likes, survey responses, or enthusiasm with demand.
- Targeting a broad persona instead of a triggered early adopter segment.
- Leading with a polished demo before breaking the old way in the prospect's mind.
- Treating customer interviews as sales calls.
- Scaling before the business model has passed demand validation.
- Asking future-tense questions and treating the answers as demand.
- Asking customers to rank the founder's problem list.
- Building a dashboard, feature, or tool because the founder heard the keyword they wanted to hear.
- Interviewing people who are not current users of the old way.

## Quality Rubric
| Criterion | Acceptable | Strong | Savant |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem Evidence | Names a plausible pain | Shows recent customer behavior | Identifies triggered, costly, current struggle with workarounds |
| Customer Forces | Lists pains and benefits | Maps push, pull, inertia, friction | Quantifies which force blocks or drives the switch |
| MVP Definition | Defines a small product | Defines problem, prospect, promise, price, package | Shows the ordered dependencies between all five P decisions |
| Validation Design | Suggests interviews or tests | Uses staged evidence gates | Converts each unknown into the smallest behavior test |
| Pricing Logic | Guesses a price | Anchors to alternatives | Ties price to economic pain, segment, and commitment threshold |
| Learning Velocity | Produces tasks | Produces experiments | Produces a weekly decision engine with kill, pivot, or proceed gates |
| Founder Discipline | Encourages action | Prevents overbuilding | Removes emotional relief until the evidence earns the next build step |
| Question Framing | Asks general questions | Uses past-tense behavioral prompts | Reconstructs the full trigger-to-choice story without leading |
| Insight Audit | Summarizes customer comments | Separates fact from interpretation | Ties every product/offer decision to transcript-grounded evidence |
| Buying Prediction | Guesses likely features | Extracts buying criteria | Predicts purchase by mapping trigger, old-way failure, alternatives, anxiety, and commitment |

# 🏙️ Rank & Rent Asset Generator (v2.0 - Elevated)

> **"Digital Real Estate is the new oil."** – Based on the *Words At Scale* "Locus Pilot" methodology.
> **v2.0 (2026-02-05)**: Engines upgraded with Harry Dry "Concrete Copy" and Oren "Taste Mastery" principles.

This skill upgrades you into a **Digital Landlord**. It provides the intelligence to find "Search Gaps" (weak competitors) and the engineering to instantly build "Asset-Class" websites that conquer those gaps.

## 🧠 The Capabilities
### 1. 🕵️ Market Espionage (The "Spy" Layer)
*Replicates: EMD Striker*
- **Capability**: Analyzes Google SERPs to find "Weak Spots" (forums, directories, outdated sites).
- **Metric**: Uses the **Striker Score** (0-100) to validate if a niche is worth entering.
- **Commands**: `/spy-market`, `/spy-amazon`.

# Attention Hijack Hooks

This companion skill turns Diandra Escobar's hook-format method into a universal hook and attention-anchor system. It extends the existing Diandra and Farrice content stacks without replacing them.

Use it when a piece of content needs:

- stronger hooks
- brand tracking or brandjack angle selection
- newsjack or trendjack angle selection
- namejack or expert-reference hooks
- rehooking a draft that has substance but weak top-of-post pull
- platform-agnostic adaptation for LinkedIn, X/Threads, newsletters, short scripts, ads, carousels, or landing-page sections

## Source Grounding
Primary source package:

- `extractions/video-context/Zc4E_K48v48/analysis.md`
- `extractions/video-context/Zc4E_K48v48/video-context-ledger.md`
- `extractions/video-context/Zc4E_K48v48/transcript.txt`
- `extractions/video-context/Zc4E_K48v48/uncertainty-report.md`

Do not claim visual or on-screen evidence from this video unless a later full-mode package adds frames or OCR rows.

## Core Thesis
The hook is not a clever line. It is the first attention contract between a reader, a platform model, and a payload.

Attention anchors create recognition. Hook formats create above-fold packaging. The curiosity gap creates the click. Human judgment chooses what deserves to be amplified.

## Available Workflows
| # | Workflow | Produces | Use When |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | [Signal Anchor Scan](workflows/01-signal-anchor-scan.md) | Ranked brand/news/name/trend/claim anchors with fit and risk notes | You need brand tracking, newsjacking, or hijackable signal ideas before drafting |
| 02 | [Hookable Elements Extractor](workflows/02-hookable-elements-extractor.md) | Hookable elements from a draft, source, transcript, offer, or raw thought | You have source material but do not know what should go above the fold |
| 03 | [Four-Format Hook Generator](workflows/03-four-format-hook-generator.md) | Dense, Punchy plus Context, Single-Line Bomb, Stacked, and Hybrid hook candidates | You need usable hook options without generic hook formulas |
| 04 | [Platform Fit Gate](workflows/04-platform-fit-gate.md) | Mobile/fold/readability audit with deterministic hook checks | A hook must survive LinkedIn or another platform's first-screen constraints |
| 05 | [Content Bridge](workflows/05-content-bridge.md) | Hook-to-content handoff for posts, scripts, newsletters, ads, carousels, or full content packs | A selected hook should become end-to-end content |

## Stacking Guide
| Stack With | Role |
|---|---|
| `/farrice-content-os` | Use as Hook Room and brand/news/name/trend anchor engine inside end-to-end content production |
| `/diandra-linkedin-system` | Use as hook writing and first-50 upgrade layer inside the LinkedIn OS |
| `/diandra-first-50` | Use after hook selection to check LinkedIn semantic signal |
| `/kallaway-trend-hook-engine` | Use when trend/outlier research should precede hook generation |
| `/high-taste-writing-os` | Use after hook selection when the draft still feels generic, flat, or AI-shaped |
| `/publishable-copy-gate` | Use before public, revenue-facing, or client-facing publication |

## Quality Gate
Reject or revise if:

- The output summarizes the attention anchor instead of extracting a point of view.
- The hook has a format but no curiosity gap.
- The hook is generic enough to fit any niche.
- The first 40 to 50 words lack topical signal for the target platform.
- The selected format ignores platform rendering, spacing, or first-screen constraints.
- The workflow claims a brand/news/person/trend fact without source evidence or an unavailable-state note.
- AI-generated options replace human judgment instead of giving the operator stronger starting points.

## Core Genius
This system combines Diandra Escobar's attention-redirection philosophy with her 2026 hook-format study. The useful leap is that brandjacking, newsjacking, namejacking, trendjacking, and draft rehooking are all the same underlying operation:

1. Find the signal that already has attention.
2. Attach it to a real payload.
3. Open a gap between expectation and claim.
4. Package that gap inside the first platform-visible window.
5. Use human judgment to choose the hook that deserves amplification.

## Source-Backed Patterns
### Pattern 1: Dual Audience Hooking

Every hook serves two audiences: the human deciding whether to keep reading and the platform model deciding whether the post deserves distribution. A strong hook cannot only be emotional; it also needs semantic signal.

### Pattern 2: Attention Anchor First

Before generating hooks, identify the attention anchor: brand, person, news, trend, claim, number, belief, artifact, or body insight. If there is no anchor, the hook has to create all recognition from scratch.

### Pattern 3: Gap Before Format

Dense, Punchy plus Context, Single-Line Bomb, Stacked, and Hybrid are packaging options. The engine is the gap between what the reader expects and what the post will claim.

### Pattern 4: Pixel/Fold Reality

On LinkedIn, the practical first-screen budget is visual, not only character-based. Hooks need width, line-break, and first-50-word checks before they are trusted.

### Pattern 5: Context Creates Better Hooks

Do not ask for hooks from a thin topic label. Give the system the draft, source, offer, audience, and payload so it can identify hookable elements instead of inventing disconnected bait.

### Pattern 6: Judgment Over Automation

AI can generate stronger starting points, but the operator must choose, combine, cut, or rewrite based on audience, voice, and taste.

## Hidden Knowledge
- A brand or news item is not the idea. It is the doorway into the idea.
- A hook that can be used by any creator is usually not specific enough for one creator.
- Punchy plus Context is the default workhorse, but overuse turns it into wallpaper.
- Dense hooks work when context itself creates tension.
- Single-Line Bomb hooks should be rare because they spend all above-fold real estate on one sentence.
- Stacked hooks fail when the lines are not part of the same series.
- The safest universal workflow is body first, hook second, format third, platform check fourth.

## Quality Rubric
| Criterion | Score 4 | Score 7 | Score 10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Signal Anchor | A recognizable source is named | The anchor has audience overlap and a clear reason to care | The anchor creates recognition, timeliness, and boomerang or debate potential |
| Payload Fit | The hook points to a general topic | The hook leads into a real argument or useful lesson | The hook makes the payload feel inevitable and worth reading now |
| Curiosity Gap | Mild intrigue | Clear expectation-versus-claim tension | Reader needs the next line because the gap hits a private belief |
| Format Choice | One format is used | Format matches the type of tension | Format, spacing, and rhythm make the hook feel native to the platform |
| Platform Fit | Roughly short enough | Survives first-screen constraints | Uses line breaks, width, first-50 signal, and mobile view deliberately |
| Judgment | Many options, no decision | Top choice with reason | Chosen hook plus rejected hooks teaches the operator how to improve future hooks |

## Anti-Patterns
1. Summary bait: naming a brand or event without a point of view.
2. Generic hook formulas: "Most people do X" without specific stakes.
3. Format cosplay: using line breaks or punchy spacing while the idea stays weak.
4. Disconnected bait: hook promises a fight the body cannot pay off.
5. AI option dump: many hooks with no scoring, no winner, and no taste call.
6. Platform denial: ignoring mobile fold, line breaks, first-50 signal, or channel norms.
