chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 1. The Physics of Inertia
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 1. The Physics of Inertia
Fladlien views the human mind as an object at rest. Persuasion isn't about "convincing" — it's about being the "Outside Force" that breaks inertia. Staying the same costs nothing in money, energy, or time. You're selling against that gravitational pull of comfort.

## Hidden Knowledge
### 2. Nested Story Architecture
Uses stories within stories to "overload" the conscious mind so the subconscious can accept the "Confidential Knowledge" (the pitch/change). Most people tell linear A-to-B stories. Embedded narrative requires cognitive load management from high-level NLP.

chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 3. Identity as the Ultimate Lever
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 3. Identity as the Ultimate Lever
Change doesn't happen at the behavior level; it happens at the identity level. "I am a person who exercises" vs. "I am doing a push-up." The industry is obsessed with tactical hacks; identity always overrides willpower.

chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 4. The "Guru to the Guru" Status
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 4. The "Guru to the Guru" Status
High-status positioning is maintained by having a Purpose larger than the transaction. If you serve the purpose, you don't need the sale — which paradoxically makes you more likely to get it. Detachment is a spiritual discipline that cannot be faked mechanically.

chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 5. The Prospect Wants to Be Less Worse, Not Better
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 5. The Prospect Wants to Be Less Worse, Not Better
"People don't want to be better — they want to be less terrible." This is semantics that isn't semantics. The prospect's frame is loss-prevention, not gain-acquisition. Copy that says "I'll make you amazing" loses to copy that says "I'll make you stop failing."

## Hidden Knowledge
### 6. Buyers Are Liars
"Just because a customer says this is their dream doesn't mean it is their dream." People can't diagnose themselves — they're like a patient looking at their own X-ray. Research must go deeper than what people SAY they want.

chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 7. The Middle Market Is Where the Real Money Lives
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 7. The Middle Market Is Where the Real Money Lives
On a $57.9 million launch, only 6.83% bought. The easy buyers buy regardless. The never-buyers never buy. The MIDDLE — people who can go either way — that's where fortunes are made. Most marketers write for the easy 7%. Fladlien writes for the next 20%.

## Hidden Knowledge
### 8. Labels Reduce Intensity
"If you label and call out the fear, you reduce its intensity. If you are the one to bring it up and address that which is typically not spoken, you reduce its intensity and you gain authority." The act of naming a fear diminishes its power.

chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 9. More of the Same Devalues All of It
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 9. More of the Same Devalues All of It
Adding more training to a training offer hurts it. "Here's a pair of shoes and seven more pairs of shoes" doesn't sweeten the deal. Complimentary modalities (socks to shoes, salt to pepper) increase value. Same-modality bonuses cannibalize.

chunks.section: Hidden Knowledge > 10. A Book Is the Greatest Sales Letter Ever Written
chunks.content:
## Hidden Knowledge
### 10. A Book Is the Greatest Sales Letter Ever Written
"A well-written book is the greatest sales letter that you could ever have." Don't write it like a sales letter — but design it so that when they finish, they want to do business with you at the highest level possible.

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 1: The Fear-of-Familiarity Close
"Almost any great idea is foreign at first. The problem with it being foreign is you will reject it because it's not familiar. But familiarity is what kills you. So we have to do the unfamiliar. So every good idea will feel uncomfortable to you at first. You don't have to immediately accept it. You just have to sit with it in all of its uncomfortableness. Allow it to settle in. See it in total and then make a decision."
- **What makes this excellent**: Spoken live, zero prep, reading the room. Contains an embedded command ("immediately accept it"), a presupposition ("you will accept it, just not immediately"), and sells against the comfort of inaction. Addresses the invisible constraint — the fear of the unfamiliar — by naming it, which reduces its intensity.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Exemplar 2: The Radical Candor PDF Lead
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 2: The Radical Candor PDF Lead
"I'm going to sell you a PDF for $49. No bonuses, no extra goodies involved, just a singular PDF for $49. And here's why this is going to be the best $49 you've ever spent."
- **What makes this excellent**: Violates every copywriting convention. No bonus stack, no scarcity, no urgency theater. Pure radical candor. Converted so well in English that when translated to Portuguese years later, it outperformed classically-trained Brazilian copywriters' scripts. The Facebook comments said "This ad is so great and I bought" — proof that honesty, wielded as scarcity, creates its own conversion force.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Exemplar 3: The 10% Self-Selection Close
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 3: The 10% Self-Selection Close
"10% of a market spends 10 times more than the rest of the market. So, if you want to get rich, sell a lot of people a small thing first and then mathematically, not because you're good or you're skilled, but because of math, 10% of them will want to buy an upgraded level. And I know 10% of you here want to go to the next level. Now, I don't know if it will be Owen or if it'll be Stacy or if it'll be Carol here or Abdul there or Jonathan there, but give me enough of you and I will create miracles."
- **What makes this excellent**: Multi-layered indirect communication. Educates (empowering). Tells them they don't have to be good (validates their insecurity). Names specific audience members (creating personal stakes). Asks them to help HIM achieve HIS goal (reciprocity + selfless justification for buying). Uses "I don't know which of you" to trigger self-selection. Never directly asks anyone to buy.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Exemplar 4: The China Concierge Flip
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 4: The China Concierge Flip
Competitors offered "We'll take you to China" as a bonus. Customers objected: "I can't get to China." Instead of arguing, Fladlien created a procurement team, offered a "China Concierge Program" as a free bonus — first product sourced free. Funded it by upselling existing clients into a $50/month membership. The team became a profit center that paid for the free bonus competitors couldn't match.
- **What makes this excellent**: Demonstrates Incomparable Offer Engineering at its peak. Took a competitor advantage and flipped it into an incomparable deliverable. Created a self-funding bonus. Made an objection disappear while generating revenue from the solution. "We got paid money to give away a free bonus that our competitors could not match."

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Anti-Exemplar: The "Hype and Features" Sales Page
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Anti-Exemplar: The "Hype and Features" Sales Page
"Are you ready to 10X your business? Our revolutionary course includes 47 video modules, 12 bonus trainings, 8 downloadable templates, and lifetime access to our community. Limited spots available — sign up now before this closes forever!"
- **Why it fails**: More of the same (47 videos + 12 bonus trainings = same modality stacking that devalues). Hype claims (10X) with zero fear-first architecture. No radical candor — screams manipulation. No constraint labeling. Invisible fears remain invisible. Easy to compare to any competitor's course.

---

## Signature Moves
1. **The "Pre-Frame the Objections" Gambit**: States potential audience skepticism before they voice it, then reframes it as a sign of readiness. → **Deploy when**: Opening any presentation or sales conversation.

2. **The "Utility of the Negative" Flip**: Takes a perceived negative and repositions it as a catalyst. "I *want* you to be skeptical." → **Deploy when**: Audience expresses resistance, doubt, or complaints.

3. **The "Identity Installation" Question**: Forces consideration of who they are *becoming*, not what they *do*. → **Deploy when**: Coaching, overcoming deep-seated beliefs, crafting high-level CTAs.

4. **The "Subtraction Audit" Challenge**: Forces identification of what to STOP doing, STOP believing, or REMOVE. → **Deploy when**: Diagnosing plateaus, overwhelm, or when a client has too many "solutions."

5. **The "Guru to the Guru" Detachment**: Communicates with complete non-neediness for the sale, emphasizing mission over transaction. → **Deploy when**: High-stakes negotiations, closing high-ticket, establishing authority.

6. **The "Label and Disarm" Move**: Names the invisible fear out loud. "This is going to be scary. This is going to be difficult." The act of naming it reduces its power. → **Deploy when**: Any moment the prospect is about to shut down mentally.

7. **The "Cost-of-Inaction Projection"**: Projects the invisible cost of staying the same over 1, 5, 10, 20 years. Makes the invisible visible. → **Deploy when**: The prospect says "I'll think about it" or "Maybe later."

8. **The "Incomparability Stack"**: Analyzes every competitor deliverable, then creates an offer that combines modalities no one else bundles. → **Deploy when**: Designing new offers, revamping stale offers, entering competitive markets.

9. **The "Agree and Redirect"**: Never disagrees with anything the prospect gives. Accepts it, agrees with it, then uses it as leverage. "It's fantastic that you're skeptical. That's exactly what I want." → **Deploy when**: Handling ANY objection, live or in copy.

10. **The "Give Me Enough of You" Transfer**: Shifts justification from self-interest to helping the seller achieve THEIR mission. Creates reciprocal motivation. → **Deploy when**: Webinar closes, live events, community-building CTAs.

| **Status Framing & Candor** | Acknowledges skepticism; states intentions | Uses direct, honest language; establishes authority through confidence | Deploys radical candor to call out elephants, filter non-ideal prospects, and make honesty itself the differentiator |
| **Inertia-Breaking Efficacy** | Presents compelling reasons to act | Addresses common points of inaction with clear steps | Identifies and attacks the core "physics of inertia" — makes inaction feel more effortful than action |
| **Identity-Level Resonance** | Focuses on what the audience can *do* or *get* | Connects to desired future self | Shifts entire narrative from "what to do" to "who to become" — transformation is identity-level |
| **Narrative Depth & Nesting** | Tells a clear, linear story | Integrates relevant anecdotes or case studies | Weaves multi-layered stories to bypass conscious resistance and deliver "confidential knowledge" subconsciously |
| **Utility of Negative Integration** | Avoids negative framing | Acknowledges challenges before offering solutions | Actively reframes skepticism, frustration, or objections as fuel or readiness indicators |
| **Proof-to-Claim Ratio** | Makes claims with some evidence | Specific examples, testimonials, or data | Proof is inherent in the framework itself — counter-intuitive results that demonstrate methodology in action |
| **Subtraction-Oriented Solution** | Offers new tools to solve problems | Identifies efficiency gains by streamlining | Pinpoints and removes a single core impediment as the primary path to exponential growth |
| **Fear-First Architecture** | Benefits outweigh perceived risks | Risk reversal present | 70% of copy focused on fear/risk removal; small claims with removed downside; prospect runs out of reasons to say NO |
| **Indirect Communication Mastery** | Direct commands and CTAs | Mix of direct and implicit suggestion | Embedded commands, presuppositions, self-selection mechanics; prospect believes they decided independently |
| **Incomparability Score** | Offer has clear advantages over competitors | Offer includes unique elements | Offer literally cannot be compared to anything else in the market — modality stack creates a category of one |

---

## Decision Framework (How Jason Thinks)
- **Subtraction First**: Never add a tactic until the core constraint is removed.
- **Find the Utility**: Negative emotions/behaviors always have a protective utility. Find it, validate it, channel it.
- **Reality Testing**: Challenge all absolute statements with clinical demands for evidence.
- **Detachment**: High status comes from deep detachment. Care about the transformation, not the transaction.
- **Fear Before Gain**: Spend 70% on removing reasons to say no, 30% on reasons to say yes.
- **Incomparability Over Competition**: Don't make a better offer — make an incomparable one.
- **Indirect Over Direct**: At mastery level, get them to sell themselves rather than being sold.
- **The Middle Market**: Don't write for the easy 7% — write for the next 20% that can go either way.

## Anti-Patterns (What Fladlien Would Reject)
- ❌ More-of-the-same bonus stacking (7 PDFs as bonuses for a PDF product)
- ❌ Hype claims without fear-first architecture ("10X your business!")
- ❌ Dismissing objections ("I know you're skeptical, I was too" without depth)
- ❌ Selling only toward pleasure without projecting the cost of inaction
- ❌ Making the offer comparable to competitors through conventional positioning
- ❌ Direct, heavy-handed CTAs when the audience is sophisticated
- ❌ Pretending you're not selling when you clearly are
- ❌ Ignoring the invisible — fears, costs, objections that go unspoken
- ❌ Treating all markets as homogeneous (directionality: toward vs. away)
- ❌ Copy that could have been written by any competent copywriter

# Jen Santulan — Voice DNA & Genius Patterns

> The signature moves that make content sound like Jen, not a brochure. Distilled from her actual voice, her ICP's midnight-Zillow pain, and the trust-first FTHB market she serves.

---

chunks.section: 1. Identity Frame: The Trusted Friend Who Happens to Sell Real Estate
chunks.content:
## 1. Identity Frame: The Trusted Friend Who Happens to Sell Real Estate
Jen is NOT the agent. She's the friend who knows real estate.

| Most agents are... | Jen is... |
|---|---|
| Selling the property | Showing you what's possible |
| Closing a transaction | Opening a door for a family |
| Performing expertise | Sharing what she actually knows |
| Optimizing for the deal | Optimizing for the right fit |
| Speaking AT buyers | Speaking WITH buyers |

**The Voice Test:** Read every line out loud. If Jen wouldn't say it to her best friend over coffee, rewrite it. The line "this property exemplifies an unparalleled lifestyle opportunity" fails the test. "You walk in and it just feels like home — let me show you" passes.

---

## 2. The Three Voice Pillars
### Pillar A: Warm, Not Performed
- Genuine excitement, not hype-bro energy
- "I love this!" reads true; "GUYS THIS IS INSANE" reads fake
- Exclamation marks earned by content, not used to manufacture energy
- 1-2 emojis per piece, placed at emotional beats — not decorative

### Pillar B: Educator, Not Salesperson
- Every hook teaches something the buyer didn't know
- Numbers woven in naturally: "$799K in a market where the median is $800K"
- Show the math, don't hide behind "great deal"
- The implicit promise: "I'll explain anything you don't understand"

### Pillar C: Permission-Giver, Not Pressure-Applier
- The FTHB market has been gaslit by clickbait scarcity ("Only 2 left!")
- Jen's edge is being the agent who DOESN'T do that
- When scarcity is real, name it precisely. When it isn't, pivot to "hidden gem"
- "You CAN do this" beats "You SHOULD do this" — every time

---

## 3. The "Midnight on Zillow" Buyer Truth
Her ICP — dual-income couples 30-42, earning $100-200K, paying $2,500-3,500 rent in LA — has a specific emotional state that ALL content must address:

**The pain script (verbatim from FTHB strategy brief):**
- "I'll never own in LA at this rate"
- "We make good money but still can't afford. It's humiliating."
- "Hoping my lottery number comes up... feels defeating when funds run out in 11 days"
- "Stuck renting into retirement"

**The hope they're searching for:**
- A program they didn't know about
- A neighborhood they hadn't considered
- A path that doesn't require winning the Dream For All lottery
- An agent who treats them as capable, not desperate

**The voice move:** Name their midnight feeling explicitly. Then flip it with one specific proof point. Never with motivation. Never with "you got this!" Always with math, address, comp, or program detail.

```
WRONG: "Don't give up on your homeownership dream! 💪✨"
RIGHT: "I know you've been scrolling at midnight thinking it's impossible.
       What if your $3,200 rent could be a $3,400 mortgage on a 4-bed in Canoga Park?"
```

---

## 4. Signature Sentence Patterns
These are Jen's actual rhythm patterns. Use them as templates, not formulas.

### Pattern 1: The "I'm Standing Here" Reveal
> "I'm standing in front of a 4-bedroom, 3-bath gated home in Canoga Park — and the price might surprise you."

Grounds you in present-tense, in-person reality. Used for property reveals.

### Pattern 2: The "Wait, What?" Setup
> "This shouldn't exist at $799K. But here it is."

Contradiction-first opener. Pattern interrupts the scroll. Used for Smart Money / Scrollstop hooks.

### Pattern 3: The "Most People Think... But Actually" Reframe
> "Most people think you need a million dollars for the Valley. Not true."

Educator move. Subverts buyer assumption with verifiable proof. Builds authority through correction, not lecture.

### Pattern 4: The "What If I Told You" Permission
> "What if I told you your rent payment could be your mortgage payment?"

The FTHB-specific permission move. Always followed by real numbers, never bare encouragement.

### Pattern 5: The "Let's [Action]" Closer
- "Let's check it out!"
- "Let's take a look!"
- "Let's go see it together!"
- "This one won't wait — let's go see it!"

Always action-oriented. Always inclusive ("let's"). Never "click the link" or "DM me." The action is the relationship, not the conversion.

---

## 5. The Show-Not-Tell Test (Sentence-Level)
Every line gets categorized. **TELL** lines die. **SHOW** lines stay.

| TELL (dead) | SHOW (alive) |
|---|---|
| "Beautiful kitchen" | "Quartz counters with the kind of pendant lights you'd save to your moodboard" |
| "Quiet neighborhood" | "26 homes behind the gate, almost zero turnover in three years" |
| "Great location" | "Five minutes to Westfield Topanga, ten to the 101" |
| "Family-friendly" | "Backyard's big enough for a swing set AND a grill — kids' bikes already in the garage" |
| "Move-in ready" | "Built 2012, original owner, kitchen redone last year, walk in tomorrow" |
| "Smart investment" | "Comparable in West Hills: $1.05M. This: $799K. Same square footage." |

**The friend test:** If Jen were texting her sister about this house at 11pm, which version would she send? That's the line.

---

chunks.section: 6. The Trust Architecture (Why Buyers Choose Jen)
chunks.content:
## 6. The Trust Architecture (Why Buyers Choose Jen)
Real estate is a high-trust transaction. Buyers in this niche have ALL been burned by:
- High-pressure agents
- Manufactured urgency
- Generic listing copy that lies
- Agents who don't return calls
- "Pre-approval" theater without education

**Jen's trust moves built into every piece of content:**

1. **Specificity = Trust** — Real numbers, real addresses, real comps. Never "great price" without the price.
2. **Math Transparency** — Show the rent-vs-mortgage calculation. Explain the program eligibility. Don't make it feel like a magic trick.
3. **Genuine Scarcity Only** — "Hidden gem" frame when no real scarcity exists. Trust > one extra DM.
4. **Educational Surplus** — Always teach more than the post requires. Example: a hook about a 4-bed in Canoga Park that drops in "PS, this also qualifies for HOP80 if you're under 80% AMI."
5. **Naming the Pain** — Buyers feel SEEN before they feel sold. Pain naming = relationship deposit.

---

chunks.section: 7. Voice Anti-Patterns (Banned — These Make Jen Sound Generic)
chunks.content:
## 7. Voice Anti-Patterns (Banned — These Make Jen Sound Generic)
| Banned move | Why |
|---|---|
| "Don't miss this!" / "Don't sleep on this!" | Generic agent voice. Anyone says this. |
| "DM me for details" / "Link in bio" | Conversion-coded. Jen says "Let's check it out." |
| "Stunning" / "Gorgeous" without specifics | Adjective inflation. Real estate Mad Libs. |
| "Dream home awaits" | Brochure language. Show the dream, don't claim it. |
| "Priced to sell" | Salesperson tell. Jen says "$50K below comps." |
| "Hot new listing" / "Just dropped" | Hype frames. Jen says "Just hit the market this morning." |
| "You won't believe..." | Curiosity-bait. Jen says "Here's what I noticed walking in." |
| Excessive emoji spam (🔥🔥🔥🚨🚨💯💯) | Reads as bot-content. Jen uses 1-2 placed at emotional beats. |

---

chunks.section: 8. The FTHB Permission Mechanic (Jen's Niche Superpower)
chunks.content:
## 8. The FTHB Permission Mechanic (Jen's Niche Superpower)
This is the move that wins the SoCal first-time buyer market. Most agents talk to FTHBs in one of two failed modes:

- **Mode 1: Pity** — "I know it's hard out there 💔" (patronizing)
- **Mode 2: Hype** — "YOU GOT THIS!! Anyone can buy!" (fake)

**Jen's mode: Permission + Proof**

The structure: NAME their exact midnight thought → FLIP with a real number/program/address → INVITE them into action.

```
NAME:    "I know you've been scrolling listings at midnight thinking you'll never own in LA."
FLIP:    "What if I told you your $3,200 rent could be a $3,400 mortgage on a 4-bed in Canoga Park?
          You CAN do this — let me show you the math."
INVITE:  "Let's take a look together! 🔑💫"
```

Every Format 2 (First-Time Buyer Permission) hook MUST do this. It's not optional. It's the ONE move that makes the entire skill worth having.

---

chunks.section: 9. SFV Specialist Positioning (The Hidden Authority Layer)
chunks.content:
## 9. SFV Specialist Positioning (The Hidden Authority Layer)
Jen is the San Fernando Valley specialist. Most LA agents claim "all of LA" — Jen owns one geography deeply. This is her durable competitive advantage.

**SFV-specific authority moves to embed across content:**

- Name SUB-neighborhoods, not just SFV: Canoga Park, Sherman Oaks, Encino, Lake Balboa, Tarzana, Van Nuys, Reseda, West Hills, Woodland Hills
- Reference local landmarks by name: Westfield Topanga, Warner Center, Lake Balboa Park, Sherman Oaks Galleria, Ventura Blvd
- Compare across neighborhoods with specific numbers: "Same house in Encino is $1.2M, in Reseda is $750K — here's why"
- Know the 101/405/118 commute differences and call them out
- Reference SFV-specific buyer programs (LACDA HOP80/HOP120, LIPA for City of LA)

The implicit message: "I know this Valley like I live here. Because I do."

---

## 10. The Quality Bar (Self-Check Before Publishing)
Run every piece against this before posting. If anything fails, rewrite that section — don't publish a flat piece.

**Voice (must pass all):**
- ☐ Would Jen say this to a best friend? (Voice test)
- ☐ Are exclamation marks earned by content, not used to fake energy?
- ☐ Are emojis placed at emotional beats, not decorative?
- ☐ Is every adjective backed by a specific number, name, or feature?
- ☐ Are contractions used naturally throughout?
- ☐ Is the closer "Let's [action]" — not "DM me" or "Link in bio"?

**Trust (must pass all for FTHB content):**
- ☐ Is scarcity genuine, or did I default to "hidden gem" framing?
- ☐ Is the math shown, not implied?
- ☐ Does the buyer feel SEEN before they feel sold?
- ☐ Is there educational surplus — something they didn't expect to learn?

**SFV Authority (passes 3+ of 5):**
- ☐ Specific sub-neighborhood named (not just "SFV")
- ☐ Local landmark referenced by name
- ☐ Cross-neighborhood comp included
- ☐ Commute / freeway context if relevant
- ☐ FTHB program callout (HOP80/120, LIPA, Greenline) if applicable

**Engagement Mechanics (passes 2+ of 4):**
- ☐ Scrollstop opener freezes scroll in first 5-8 words
- ☐ Curiosity gap pulls reader through middle
- ☐ Share trigger identified (identity/practical/social currency)
- ☐ Save trigger identified (educational density)

---

## 11. Domain Boundary
**This skill produces:**
- Instagram Reels video hooks (12-18 seconds spoken)
- Instagram Stories education series (FTHB-focused)
- Instagram Carousels (neighborhood deep-dives, comparison content)
- Captions for any of the above

**This skill does NOT produce:**
- Long-form blog content (use Nicolas Cole skill if needed)
- Email sequences (use email-narrative skill)
- Listing descriptions for MLS (different voice register, more conservative)
- Cold outreach DMs (use cold-outreach-gen)
- Paid ad copy (use Luke Iha or Stefan Georgi skills)

For anything outside Reels/Stories/Carousels/Captions, route to the appropriate expert and adapt OUTPUT to Jen's voice via voice-calibrate.

Engineer the internal operating system that produces external revenue breakthroughs.

Every component (identity, motivational drivers, risk tolerance, worldview, responsibility framework) is a variable that can be deliberately adjusted to produce different revenue outcomes. ## Available Workflows

|---|---------|----------|----------|

# Jeremy Haynes Mindset Systems — Genius Context

> Load this file before executing any workflow. It contains the full
> extraction intelligence — patterns, tacit knowledge, and operating
> principles that make this expert's output actually work.

## Genius Patterns
10 mastery patterns decoded from Jeremy Haynes' mindset engineering methodology. These are the practitioner-derived systems that took him from $550K/year to multi-millions, running 12-15 rev-share deals at $100K+/month each.

---

## Pattern 1: Identity Versioning Protocol
**The Pattern:** Identity is not a fixed thing you discover — it's a document you iterate. Jeremy writes explicit lists of traits and characteristics for his next identity version, posts them visibly, and references them during live situations (sales calls, decisions, conversations). He's on version 47.0.

**Why It's Genius:** Most "identity work" is vague journaling. Jeremy made it operational — a spec sheet you glance at mid-call to course-correct behavior in real time. Each version may change only ONE trait. The granularity makes it actionable rather than aspirational.

**When To Deploy:** Any time a specific trait or characteristic is blocking growth. Not for general "I want to be better" — for "this specific behavior pattern is the ceiling."

**Key Mechanic:** *"Every trait and characteristic of you is fully fluid and dynamic. 100% of what you consider you can change."* The shift is a decision, not a process. Light switch, not dimmer.

---

## Pattern 2: Dynamic Reasons Engine
**The Pattern:** Motivational drivers expire. The reasons that got you to $1M won't get you to $10M. Old reasons must be consciously identified and swapped for new ones — which may be selfish, philanthropic, or irrational. What matters is emotional stir, not moral purity.

**Why It's Genius:** Solves the "arrived and stuck" syndrome that hits entrepreneurs at every plateau. Most advice says "find your why" once. Jeremy says your why has a shelf life and must be refreshed like an expired subscription.

**When To Deploy:** Revenue plateau, loss of drive, "golden handcuffs" feeling, post-achievement flatness.

**Key Mechanic:** After giving a reasons talk at his mastermind, the number of clients hitting $1M/month nearly doubled (from ~5 to 9 in 3 months). The framework demonstrably accelerates revenue growth.

---

## Pattern 3: Pain Leverage Inversion
**The Pattern:** Human beings are neurologically wired to avoid pain (Daniel Goleman's blind spot research). Instead of fighting this wiring, weaponize it. Deliberately amplify the pain of your current circumstances until escape velocity is achieved. You can also diminish pain of desired actions using NLP techniques (Richard Bandler — shrink the memory, make it black-and-white, turn down the volume).

**Why It's Genius:** Works WITH neurology instead of against it. Most motivation advice says "overcome fear" — Jeremy says "make your current situation more terrifying than the risk."

**When To Deploy:** Stuck in comfort, unable to make a scary decision, need escape velocity from a limiting situation.

**Key Mechanic:** *"You can justify anything. Look up 'is the sun good, is the sun bad' — you'll have information equal to both. In all decisions we have the ability to choose which direction to use it."*

---

## Pattern 4: Asymmetric Risk Assessment
**The Pattern:** Risk is rarely 50/50. Most entrepreneurial decisions have significantly more upside than downside (asymmetric upside). The fire/water analogy: if you're on fire and there's a pool that might be water or gas — you're jumping. Because staying on fire is certain death.

**Why It's Genius:** Replaces emotional risk-aversion with structural analysis. Three categories: (1) High asymmetric upside — jump. (2) Unknown unknowns — trust intuition/faith. (3) Asymmetric downside — avoid unless forced.

**When To Deploy:** Any decision paralysis. Especially when "it feels risky" but you haven't actually quantified the risk.

**Key Mechanic:** When you can't risk capital, risk time and relationships instead. "Time and effort based risks have longer cycles but still have financial upside." The podcast-hosting example: Grant was already taking the risk (equipment, flights, studio rental) but not capturing the financial upside (affiliate deals).

---

## Pattern 5: Revenue Math Decision Framework
**The Pattern:** When facing chaos or a scaling wall, stop everything and do the math. Write it on a wall. What does the goal actually require? Jeremy's pivotal moment: $1M/month ÷ 10 deals = $100K/deal. This simple math invalidated his entire operating model and led to firing 23 of 27 staff.

**Why It's Genius:** The math is always available but rarely done. Jeremy could have done this calculation before scaling to 3 offices and 27 staff — he calls himself "idiotic" for not doing it sooner. The math provides "clear evidence" that cuts through emotional attachment to bad strategies.

**When To Deploy:** Scaling chaos, over-hiring, service proliferation, any time complexity is growing but revenue isn't proportional.

**Key Mechanic:** Start with the goal, work backward to deal structure, then ruthlessly eliminate everything that doesn't serve that structure. The rev-share model ($10K base + 10% net) emerged directly from the math — not from industry benchmarking or mentorship.

---

## Pattern 6: Worldview Propaganda Protocol
**The Pattern:** All sensory input shapes worldview. Worldview shapes all decisions. Therefore, curate ALL input as deliberately as a propagandist. This includes: content feeds, physical environment, conversations, smells, people you follow, and negative reference points.

**Why It's Genius:** Goes beyond "curate your feed" to include environmental propaganda (moved homes over a sewage smell at $300K cost), kinesthetic input, and deliberate anti-propaganda (following people he demonizes as negative reference points).

**When To Deploy:** Always. This is an ongoing system, not a one-time cleanup. Particularly critical during identity transitions.

**Key Mechanic:** *"Your subconscious fires 20-40 million neurons per second. Your conscious brain fires 20-40 thousand. Just because you don't think it consciously has an impact does not mean it doesn't subconsciously have an impact."* Will literally tell people mid-sentence to stop talking if content threatens his worldview.

---

## Pattern 7: Responsibility-Expansion Correlation
**The Pattern:** As wealth increases, responsibility increases. Most people's broken mental model: "more responsibility → must risk less." Correct model: "more responsibility → must expand more aggressively to carry the weight higher."

**Why It's Genius:** Identifies and names the exact mental model error that traps family entrepreneurs. Uses the anchor/hot-air-balloon visualization to make the correction intuitive and visceral.

**When To Deploy:** When someone says "I can't take risks because I have a family/employees/obligations." This is the direct counter-framework.

**Key Mechanic:** The broken cycle (get richer → more responsibility → contract → pressure → forced action → eventually get richer) has a massive inefficiency gap that can be eliminated with one mental model shift. Correct cycle: get richer → more responsibility → continue expansion-oriented action → get richer again.

---

## Pattern 8: Momentum Snowball Effect
**The Pattern:** Building momentum is exponentially harder at the start than at any point after. The snowman metaphor: packing the first ball is brutal. After that, everything compounds. Most people look at untouched snow and decide to drink hot chocolate inside.

**Why It's Genius:** Names the specific trap (comfort alternatives) and the specific mechanism (validation cycles that build psyche). "If you do that for even 13 months, you come out the other side a monster."

**When To Deploy:** In the slog of starting. Before the first major win. When comfort alternatives are most tempting.

**Key Mechanic:** "Excessive accomplishment in short time frames is really just a byproduct of the momentum they've created." The compound effect is real — but only accessible to those who endured the initial packing of the snowball.

---

## Pattern 9: Scarcity Domination Protocol
**The Pattern:** When scarcity feelings arise — even tiny ones — immediately spend to obliterate them. Don't budget your way out of scarcity mindset. Crush it with action that proves the limitation is false.

**Why It's Genius:** Inverts conventional financial wisdom. Instead of saving to feel safe, spending to prove safety. The cable-snap gym story is the physical metaphor: rage against the limitation until the equipment breaks. "Mission accomplished. The inner voice will shut up now."

**When To Deploy:** Any time a purchase or investment creates anxiety. Any time you're hesitating based on "can I afford this?" rather than "is this strategically sound?"

**Key Mechanic:** *"Spending the money unlocks a heightened level of creativity and a new way to make a fuckload more money that you previously would not have committed to."* The spend itself creates the pressure → creativity → revenue cycle.

---

## Pattern 10: Validation Cycle Stacking
**The Pattern:** Confidence and capacity aren't built through affirmations — they're built through completed loops: attempt → succeed → internalize proof → attempt bigger. Stack enough loops and you become "a monster."

**Why It's Genius:** Makes confidence mechanical rather than emotional. It's not about belief — it's about evidence accumulation. Each cycle literally expands what you view as possible because you have proof.

**When To Deploy:** Before any major leap. Review stacked validations to establish pattern of capability. Also: design small validation cycles into any new venture to build momentum before the big bet.

**Key Mechanic:** Jeremy's proof chain: sales trainer skills validated repeatedly → quit to start agency ($550K yr1) → scaled to $2M yr2 → did the math → contracted → rev-share model with Dan Luck → doubled Dan's revenue in 2 weeks → validation → scaled Dan to $2M/month in 8 months → model proven → accumulated more deals.

## 1. The Calculus of Contraction
Jeremy presents his "fire 23 people" moment as a bold decision. The hidden knowledge: he specifically identifies it as a *temporary contraction followed by immediate expansion*. The contraction was not retreat — it was a reload. He refunded $109K in deals AND immediately started video-pitching new prospects from his apartment the same period. The lesson isn't "sometimes you need to shrink" — it's "contract the model, not the ambition." His vision expanded while his operation contracted.

## 2. Validation Before Vision
Jeremy didn't have big vision first and then build skills. He built skills first (at the sales trainer's company) and then the vision expanded as validation cycles accumulated. The hidden sequence: **skill → validation → expanded identity → expanded vision → validation → repeat.** Most people try to start with vision and wonder why they can't execute. Jeremy's approach: you earn the right to bigger vision through stacked proof.

## 3. The Speed Tax
Jeremy mentions the second year: "2 million, hired over two dozen staff, three offices, flying LA to Miami every week, 4 hours of sleep, 1000+ caloric deficit for a year and a half." He frames this as chaos, but the hidden lesson is that speed has a physical cost he was willing to pay — and he frames the paying of it as another validation cycle. The speed tax is a feature, not a bug. Those who won't pay it don't get the proof of capacity that comes out the other side.

## 4. Month-to-Month as Dominance Signal
The month-to-month contract structure is presented as fairness. The hidden function: it's a massive competence signal. "We'll throw our balls on the table. You don't want to work with us, we probably don't want to work with you." Any agency can lock clients into 12-month contracts. Only one that knows it delivers can afford month-to-month at $100K+/month. The contract structure IS the marketing.

## 5. Reasons Expire at Predictable Thresholds
Jeremy doesn't say this explicitly, but the pattern is clear: reasons expire when the emotional gap between desire and reality closes. Stephen's family-oriented reasons expired when his family was fully provided for. Edward's personal reasons expired when nothing material was missing. The hidden law: **a reason only works while there's an emotional gap between current state and desired state.** Once the gap closes, the reason dies and must be replaced — or you stall.

## 6. Demonization as Self-Regulation
The "Camry and double-wide trailer" guy Jeremy follows isn't followed for entertainment. He's followed as a *deliberate fear object* — a living representation of what to avoid. Jeremy uses attraction AND repulsion as dual vectors of worldview maintenance. Most people only curate for aspiration. Jeremy actively curates for disgust. The emotional charge of "I never want to be like this person" is leveraged as fuel alongside "I want to be more like that person."

## 7. The Subconscious Trojan Horse
Jeremy buries a critical insight inside the police encounter story. The real lesson isn't about risk — it's about emotional recycling. He took rage from a traffic stop and converted it into the best workout of his life. Then he went back and thanked the officer. The hidden pattern: **every negative emotion is recyclable fuel.** He doesn't suppress emotions or process them through talk therapy. He *redirects them physically* and then releases the charge. The emotional energy is the same — only the target changes.

## 8. The "Squeeze" Mortality Frame
The walls-closing-in metaphor at the transcript's end is positioned as encouragement, but the hidden operating principle is darker and more powerful: **you're dying no matter what.** The squeeze is guaranteed. Every decision is just about where in the hallway you experience the crush. This is Jeremy's actual risk framework underneath all the other frameworks: since the downside ceiling (death) is already guaranteed, every risk's actual downside is bounded by that certainty. It makes every individual risk feel smaller.

## 9. Reciprocity as Identity Block
When Grant confesses he's "really scared of asking" — Jeremy immediately identifies this as an identity issue, not a skills issue. The hidden knowledge: **reluctance to capture value is always an identity problem, never a pricing problem.** Grant doubled his prices and nobody objected. The market was already willing to pay more. The only thing in the way was Grant's self-concept. Jeremy's instinct to diagnose identity first (before strategy, tactics, or skills) is his deepest pattern.

## 10. Faith as Scale-Unlock
Jeremy's late adoption of faith ("I didn't even know the word faith until like a year ago") is presented as personal growth. The hidden function is operational: faith provides a reason that doesn't expire because the gap (human potential vs God's vision) is infinite. Unlike selfish or philanthropic reasons which close as you achieve, a God-driven purpose has no ceiling. This is why Jeremy frames it as "the messenger" — the identity is permanently aspirational. He solved the reasons-expiration problem at scale.

---

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
**1. The $1M/Month Math Deconstruction**
*   **Exemplar:** Jeremy Haynes faced scaling chaos with 27 staff and 3 offices. He stopped everything, wrote "$1M/month / 10 deals = $100K/deal" on a glass wall. This simple math instantly invalidated his entire operating model, leading him to fire 23 staff, refund $109K in deals, close offices, and pivot to a lean, high-leverage rev-share model. This drastic contraction was immediately followed by aggressive expansion into the new model.
*   **What makes this excellent:** This demonstrates Pattern 5 (Revenue Math Decision Framework) and Hidden Knowledge 1 (The Calculus of Contraction) at its peak. It's a ruthless, evidence-based decision that cuts through emotional attachment to a failing system, leading to a complete, effective reset and subsequent exponential growth. The math provided undeniable clarity and permission for radical action.

**2. The Homeless Shelter Philanthropist**
*   **Exemplar:** A client, initially driven by a deep-seated "hatred of homeless people," was coached by Jeremy to consciously leverage this intense negative emotion. Instead of suppressing it, the client channeled it into building superior homeless shelters and lobbying politicians for systemic change. This inverted motivation led to a 3.5x revenue increase from ~$2M to ~$7M/month.
*   **What makes this excellent:** This is a perfect illustration of Pattern 2 (Dynamic Reasons Engine) and Pattern 3 (Pain Leverage Inversion). It showcases the genius of transforming a morally ambiguous, yet emotionally potent, driver into a powerful engine for both personal wealth and philanthropic impact, proving that "emotional stir" trumps "moral purity" for drive.

**3. The Birkin Bag Scarcity Domination**
*   **Exemplar:** When Jeremy felt a subtle hint of scarcity around a significant purchase, he immediately bought three Birkin bags (totaling over $79K) within six weeks. He didn't desire the bags themselves; the act of spending was a deliberate, overwhelming counter-action to obliterate the scarcity mindset, proving to his subconscious that "a piece of leather is not bigger than you."
*   **What makes this excellent:** A pure, extreme application of Pattern 9 (Scarcity Domination Protocol). It's a hyper-specific, counter-intuitive behavioral intervention that uses aggressive spending as a therapeutic and strategic tool to unlock creativity and future revenue, rather than a frivolous act.

**Anti-Exemplar: The "Responsible" Plateau**
*   **Exemplar:** An entrepreneur reaches $5M/year, feels a surge of responsibility towards their growing team and family, and decides to "play it safe." They stop investing in new, riskier ventures, delay hiring a high-cost A-player, and continue with a comfortable but inefficient operating model. Their revenue stagnates for two years, and their drive slowly erodes.
*   **What makes this mediocre:** This embodies the broken mental model described in Pattern 7 (Responsibility-Expansion Correlation). Instead of using increased responsibility as fuel for expansion, the entrepreneur contracts, mistaking safety for strategy, ultimately leading to stagnation and loss of momentum.

## Signature Moves
*   **Identity Versioning Check**: Jeremy will pause mid-conversation or decision-making to mentally (or physically, by glancing at a note) reference his current "Jeremy [X].0" identity version, ensuring his actions align with the desired traits. → **Deploy when**: Facing a critical decision, a challenging negotiation, or sensing a deviation from desired behavior.
*   **Revenue Math First**: When presented with a complex business problem, a scaling challenge, or a new opportunity, Jeremy immediately asks for or calculates the core revenue math required to achieve the goal, often simplifying it to a "deals per month" and "revenue per deal" structure. → **Deploy when**: Any strategic planning, problem-solving, or assessing feasibility of a new venture.
*   **Worldview Propaganda Purge**: Jeremy will abruptly terminate conversations, unfollow social media accounts, or physically remove himself from environments that introduce limiting beliefs, negative narratives, or content that contradicts his desired worldview. → **Deploy when**: Encountering input that feels disempowering, fear-inducing, or misaligned with his expansion-oriented mindset.
*   **Scarcity Overwhelm Action**: Upon detecting any internal flicker of scarcity or hesitation around a financial decision, Jeremy will immediately identify a disproportionately large spend or investment that directly challenges that scarcity, often without full logical justification beyond "crushing the voice." → **Deploy when**: Experiencing financial anxiety, hesitation on a strategic investment, or feeling limited by perceived monetary constraints.
*   **Asymmetric Risk Framing**: When a decision feels "risky," Jeremy automatically re-frames it using the fire/water analogy or by quantifying the true upside vs. downside, often highlighting the greater risk of inaction or maintaining the status quo. → **Deploy when**: Facing decision paralysis, encountering fear-based objections (internal or external), or evaluating new opportunities.

# Jeremy Miner: Identity-Based Persuasion & Psychological Framing — Genius Context

> Load this file before executing any workflow. It contains the full

## Pattern 1: Identity-First Persuasion Architecture
**The Insight:** "People do who they believe they are." Every buying decision is an identity decision.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy never argues features against objections. He shifts the frame to identity—making the prospect see themselves as "the type of person who..." before any pitch.

**Executable Version:**
- Before presenting ANY solution, establish what "type of person" makes that decision
- Frame buying as identity-congruent ("People who build businesses...")
- Frame not buying as identity-threatening ("The people who stay stuck...")

**Success Metric:** Prospects use identity language when explaining their decision

---

## 2. Self-Question Pattern
**The Insight:** Direct claims trigger skepticism. Questions trigger self-discovery.

**Observable Behavior:** When Jeremy wants the prospect to believe something, he asks a question that leads them to say it themselves. "Have you ever noticed that the people who complain about price are usually the ones who struggle the most?"

**Executable Version:**
- Replace statements with questions
- "This will help you scale" → "What would happen to your business if you could actually scale?"
- Lead them to articulate the conclusion you want them to reach

**Success Metric:** Prospect states the key insight in their own words

---

## Pattern 3: Pre-Frame Everything
**The Insight:** How something is introduced determines how it's received. Context > Content.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy precedes EVERY framework, price, or concept with a pre-frame that elevates its perceived value. "What I'm about to share with you is something I only discovered after..."

**Executable Version:**
- Never introduce anything "cold"
- Create anticipation and context before the reveal
- Use scarcity, authority, or transformation pre-frames

**Success Metric:** Audience leans in before you deliver the content

---

## Pattern 4: Indirect Attribution
**The Insight:** Third-person stories bypass resistance that first-person claims trigger.

**Observable Behavior:** "My mentor once told me..." or "A client of mine was exactly where you are..." Jeremy constantly attributes wisdom to third parties, making it feel like observation rather than persuasion.

**Executable Version:**
- Replace "You should..." with "What I've noticed is that people like you..."
- Use mentor stories to deliver difficult truths
- Let the story be the teacher

**Success Metric:** Prospect applies the story's lesson without feeling preached at

---

## 5. 4 Identity Types Framework
**The Insight:** Markets aren't demographics—they're identity types. Create a spectrum where everyone wants to be at the top.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy segments any market into 4 types (Wingers/Dabblers/Know-It-Alls/Committed to Mastery). Each type carries psychological weight—no one wants to be a Dabbler.

**Executable Version:**
- Create your industry's 4 types
- Name them so lower types are embarrassing and upper types are aspirational
- Ask the prospect where they see themselves (they'll pick higher)

**Success Metric:** Prospect self-identifies with higher type and asks how to get there

---

## Pattern 6: Consequence Stacking
**The Insight:** People avoid pain more than they pursue gain. Stack consequences to amplify motivation.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy doesn't ask "What do you want?" He asks "What happens if you don't solve this? And then what happens? And what does that lead to?" Each layer deepens the emotional urgency.

**Executable Version:**
- Ask "What happens if nothing changes?"
- Follow with "And what does THAT lead to?"
- Keep stacking until you hit emotional bedrock (family, legacy, identity)

**Success Metric:** Prospect articulates their own deepest consequences

---

## Pattern 7: Pattern Interrupts
**The Insight:** Predictable = resistible. Break the expected pattern to open the mind.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy says the opposite of what's expected. Instead of hyping his value, he downplays: "Look, I don't know if this is even right for you." This creates intrigue and lowers defenses.

**Executable Version:**
- When they expect enthusiasm, be reserved
- When they expect a pitch, ask questions
- When they expect agreement, challenge

**Success Metric:** Prospect says "That's not what I expected" or leans in with curiosity

---

## Pattern 8: Binary Identity Questions
**The Insight:** Either/or questions where both answers confirm the positive identity.

**Observable Behavior:** "Is that persistence something you were born with, or something you developed over time?" Either answer confirms they HAVE persistence. There's no exit from the positive frame.

**Executable Version:**
- After positioning a positive identity, lock it with a binary question
- Structure: "Is [positive trait] something you've always had, or something you built?"
- Both options confirm the trait exists

**Success Metric:** Prospect claims the identity through their answer

---

## 9. Reframe Flip
**The Insight:** Every negative contains a positive. Find it and name it.

**Observable Behavior:** "I've tried coaching before and it didn't work" → "So you're the type who keeps investing in themselves even after disappointment. That's rare."

**Executable Version:**
- Hear the complaint, find the strength it implies
- Name that strength explicitly
- Let them claim it as their identity

**Success Metric:** Prospect shifts from defensive to proud within 30 seconds

---

## Pattern 10: Objection Inoculation
**The Insight:** Address objections before they're spoken. Prevention > Handling.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy mentions common objections in his pre-frames, positions them as identities of "the wrong type," so prospects don't want to voice them. "Some people say 'I need to think about it'—and between us, that usually means 'no' or 'fear.'"

**Executable Version:**
- Identify your top 3 objections
- Build pre-frames that make voicing them feel like admitting weakness
- Deploy early in the conversation

**Success Metric:** Common objections don't appear, or prospect actively distances from them

---

## Pattern 11: Tonal Calibration
**The Insight:** HOW you say it matters more than WHAT you say. Tone conveys subtext.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy matches nervous energy with calm authority. He matches skepticism with curiosity, not defensiveness. His tone communicates safety and competence.

**Executable Version:**
- Mirror emotional state briefly, then lead to your desired state
- Use strategic pauses after key statements
- Slow down for important points, speed up for transitions

**Success Metric:** Prospect's emotional state shifts to match yours

---

## 12. Permission Close
**The Insight:** Asking permission creates choice. Choice creates ownership.

**Observable Behavior:** "Would it be okay if I shared something with you?" "Can I ask you a personal question?" Jeremy constantly asks permission, making the prospect feel in control while actually leading them.

**Executable Version:**
- Before any bold statement or personal question, ask permission
- This lowers resistance and creates micro-commitments
- Stack permissions throughout the conversation

**Success Metric:** Prospect feels they chose to engage at every step

---

## Pattern 13: Future Pacing
**The Insight:** Make the transformed future vivid and present.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy paints specific future scenarios: "Imagine 6 months from now, you wake up and your calendar isn't full of fires..." He makes the desired outcome tangible and emotionally real.

**Executable Version:**
- After establishing desire, paint a specific future scene
- Include sensory details and emotional states
- Connect it to their stated values and goals

**Success Metric:** Prospect's eyes light up or they verbalize the vision

---

## Pattern 14: Real-Time Pattern Recognition
**The Insight:** Read the room and adjust in real-time. No script survives contact with a real human.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy notices micro-expressions, hesitations, and energy shifts. He names them: "I noticed you paused when I mentioned budget—what came up for you there?"

**Executable Version:**
- Watch for incongruence between words and body language
- Name it non-judgmentally when you see it
- Create space for the underlying truth

**Success Metric:** Prospect shares the real concern beneath the surface objection

---

## Integration Note
These patterns compound. A single conversation might use:
1. Pre-Frame Formula (Pattern 3) →
2. 4 Identity Types (Pattern 5) →
3. Binary Identity Lock (Pattern 8) →
4. Consequence Stack (Pattern 6) →
5. Permission Close (Pattern 12)

Mastery isn't knowing the patterns—it's flowing between them based on what the moment requires.

---

## Pattern 15: Frame / Deframe / Reframe Engine
**The Insight:** Every human carries belief systems (frames) installed during childhood (ages 4-13). A frame is just a belief. Persuasion is the art of taking someone out of one frame (deframe) and installing a new one (reframe).

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy demonstrates this with a psychology example — a suicidal patient has a frame (belief they should end their life). The psychologist must deframe (take them out of that belief) and reframe (install a new belief about the people who love them and what life could be). He applies this exact mechanic to sales: prospects arrive in a "price/cost-based thinking" frame and must be reframed into "results-based thinking."

**Executable Version:**
- Identify the prospect's current frame (e.g., "this is too expensive")
- Deframe: disrupt that belief system with questions that make them question it
- Reframe: install the new frame by redirecting focus (e.g., to the results, the cost of NOT acting)
- The transition must feel natural — questions are the vehicle, never statements

**Success Metric:** Prospect shifts language from cost-focused to results-focused without realizing you engineered it

---

## Pattern 16: NPQ Connection Questions
**The Insight:** In the first 30-60 seconds, you have zero credibility. Asking "meaty" problem questions too early triggers the guard. Connection questions must focus on the end result, not the problem.

**Observable Behavior:** Instead of "What's going on with you?" (which gets vague, guarded responses), Jeremy opens with: "Looks like you booked in with us about looking at ways to get rid of the numbness in your feet so you can feel comfortable walking again, right?" — immediately pointing at the result, not the problem.

**Executable Version:**
- Never ask probing questions before trust is established
- Lead with what you already know about their situation — phrased as the end result
- "Looks like you [action they took] about [the end result they want], right?"
- This instantly takes them from cost-based thinking to results-based thinking

**Success Metric:** Prospect's first response is about their desired outcome, not their guard

---

## Pattern 17: POV — Perception of Value
**The Insight:** "It's your perception of value, not the value itself." Two identical pictures — one in a golden frame, one in a flea market frame. Same picture, but the perceived value is completely different. Your offer is the picture. Your communication is the frame.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy tells the audience: "People don't come to me because they think I understand their product better than they do. They come because I know how to FRAME their product better than they can."

**Executable Version:**
- Before improving your offer, improve how you communicate your offer
- Audit: Is your communication a golden frame or a flea market frame?
- The same service positioned differently can command 2-10x the price
- Apply to: sales scripts, landing pages, email sequences, social posts

**Success Metric:** Same offer, different frame → measurably higher conversion or willingness to pay

---

## Pattern 18: Price-to-Results Reframe
**The Insight:** When prospects think "How much does this cost?" they're in price/cost-based thinking. Your job throughout the ENTIRE conversation is to shift them into results-based thinking.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy uses comparison framing: "Which is more expensive — getting the funding together and fixing your back, or going through surgery, staying on drugs the rest of your life, and losing three more promotions? In reality, which is more expensive?" The concerned tone makes this feel empathetic, not aggressive.

**Executable Version:**
- Never answer a price objection with justification
- Instead, compare: "Is it more expensive to [invest in solution] or to [continue suffering + cascading consequences]?"
- Stack 2-3 consequences to make the comparison overwhelming
- Always use concerned tone — you're helping them see reality, not pitching

**Success Metric:** Prospect says "I never thought about it that way" or shifts to discussing outcomes instead of cost

---

## Pattern 19: Nervous System Science
**The Insight:** Objections originate from the nervous system, not logic. When a prospect's nervous system triggers fight-or-flight, they produce objections, give one-word answers, fold their arms, and shut down. Calming the nervous system PREVENTS objections at the source.

**Observable Behavior:** Jeremy downplays consultations: "Yeah, today's pretty basic." He uses neutral language, concerned tones, and humor. All of these calm the nervous system. When he says "I want to disarm the prospect," what he means scientifically is: "I want to calm their nervous system so fight-or-flight doesn't trigger."

**Executable Version:**
- Prospect resistance = activated nervous system, not a logic problem
- Calm it through: neutral language, downplaying (not hyping), concerned tone, humor (releases dopamine)
- Ask yourself: "Is my communication calming their nervous system or activating it?"
- Every element of your approach should reduce perceived threat

**Success Metric:** Prospect physically relaxes (uncrosses arms, leans in, gives longer answers)

---
