# Sean Mabry — Genius Patterns

> Load this file before deploying any Mabry workflow. These are the thinking patterns that make his voice methodology work — the how-he-thinks, not just what-he-does.

## Pattern 1: The Prediction Discipline
**Core Insight**: Voice mastery isn't research → replicate. It's research → **predict** → calibrate.

Most ghostwriters passively consume content and try to mimic. Mabry actively generates predictions: "What would this client say about a topic they've never addressed?" Then he checks against reality. Each wrong prediction — corrected in a review call — refines the internal mental model exponentially faster than more passive consumption would.

**Application Rule**: By Week 2 of any engagement, you should be generating 5-10 predictions per review cycle. If you can't predict, you don't have the model yet. Keep consuming until you can start guessing.

---

## Pattern 2: The Controversy Line Map
**Core Insight**: Everyone who builds a lasting personal brand has a hidden three-zone map of how they engage with controversy.

- **Zone 1 — Flag-Plant**: Core to who they are. They go hard. Use for hooks and bold hooks.
- **Zone 2 — Nuanced**: They engage carefully with caveats. Use for depth pieces.
- **Zone 3 — No-Go**: They actively avoid. Never touch this regardless of how "polarizing" advice says to be.

**Application Rule**: Young copywriters get told "be polarizing." Leaders know where the line is. Your job is to find it without them needing to teach you. Map it from their existing content — look at what they've repeated vs. what they've touched once vs. what they've conspicuously avoided.

---

## Pattern 3: The Hidden Gem Collector
**Core Insight**: The most powerful stories are the ones the client tells casually on podcasts but doesn't think to suggest for content.

Listen to every guest appearance. Flag stories that: (a) reveal character, (b) contain a concrete detail, or (c) made the host visibly react. Build a bank separate from the client's "official" story list. These hidden gems are your secret weapon for freshness — the audience hasn't heard them and the client forgot they told them.

**Application Rule**: For every client, maintain two story banks — "Their Picks" (stories they suggest) and "My Picks" (stories you found in their natural conversation). Your job is to have "My Picks" outnumber "Their Picks" by 2:1.

---

## Pattern 4: The Authorship Pyramid
**Core Insight**: A first book should capture the base of the industry pyramid (dreamers, aspirational readers), not the tactical middle.

The base becomes evangelists. The top of the pyramid (elite peers, partners) responds not to money or credentials but to **influence over the base**. Write a memoir that shows the full hero's journey — from clueless newbie to where they are now. Alex Hormozi, Dan Martell — this is exactly the pattern they executed.

**Application Rule**: If a client wants to write "no-fluff tactics" as their first book, redirect them. Tactical books start halfway up the pyramid and can't work their way down. The memoir starts at the base and lets readers project their own journey onto yours — which resonates at every level simultaneously.

---

## Pattern 5: The Mode-Split Protocol
**Core Insight**: The creative brain and the workhorse brain use identical horsepower but for opposite purposes. You cannot use both at once.

- **Workhorse mode**: Timed, clock-obsessed, Parkinson's Law applied, speed is the goal. For maintenance content — batch emails, scheduled posts, admin.
- **Deep work mode**: Clock-forgotten, immersive, no Pomodoro. If you're watching the clock, that's a signal of misalignment. For transformative projects — book chapters, new offers, creative breakthroughs.

**Application Rule**: Hemingway's "write drunk, edit sober" — not literally. The raw creative brain generates; the editor brain reduces. They have opposite purposes. Schedule them in separate blocks. Never switch back and forth mid-day.

---

## Pattern 6: The Trust Ladder
**Core Insight**: Voice writing autonomy is earned through a specific progression. Skipping stages destroys the relationship; respecting them builds irreplaceability.

Stage 1: Write → client reviews → someone else publishes.
Stage 2: Write → client reviews → you publish.
Stage 3: Write → publish without review.

**Application Rule**: The "no edits" milestone at Stage 2 is the most important moment in a voice-writing engagement. Chase it. When it happens, you've proven the mental model works. Don't rush to Stage 3 — let the client offer it when they're ready.

---

chunks.content:
## Meta-Pattern: Voice as the AI-Proof Moat
Everything above exists because voice writing is the one copywriting lane that AI cannot commoditize. AI handles templates. It cannot build a predictive mental model of a human, map their controversy boundaries, or collect their hidden gems. If you can write in voice, everything else is just a different workflow. This is the surviving lane.

---

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 1: The "100M Offers" Book Strategy (Alex Hormozi)
**Description**: Alex Hormozi's first book, "$100M Offers," isn't a dry tactical manual for advanced entrepreneurs. Instead, it starts with a clear, accessible philosophy and a compelling journey, targeting the "dreamers" and aspirational entrepreneurs at the base of the industry pyramid. It simplifies complex ideas and positions Hormozi as a guide, not just a guru. This approach made the book a viral phenomenon, creating a massive base of evangelists that then drew the attention of elite peers and partners.
**What makes this excellent**: This perfectly executes Mabry's **Authorship Pyramid** (Pattern 4). By focusing on the base, it built influence from the ground up, a strategy far more effective for a first-time author than starting with advanced tactics. It demonstrates the power of leading with a memoir-like journey (even if business-focused) to generate widespread resonance.

chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 2: The "Controversy-Calibrated" Response (Reconstructed)
**Description**: A ghostwritten newsletter addressing a recent industry shift. The client is known for strong opinions on market trends, but this specific shift involves sensitive ethical considerations where their brand needs to appear thoughtful. The piece opens with a bold, "flag-plant" statement aligning with the client's core values, then transitions into a nuanced discussion of the ethical complexities, acknowledging multiple perspectives without taking a definitive hard stance on the sensitive issue itself. It conspicuously avoids commenting on a highly polarizing sub-topic related to the shift, which the client has never publicly engaged with.
**What makes this excellent**: This demonstrates masterful application of **The Controversy Line Map** (Pattern 2). It precisely navigates the client's three zones—going hard on core values (flag-plant), engaging carefully with caveats on ethics (nuanced), and completely avoiding a no-go topic. The client feels perfectly represented, avoiding reputational risk while maintaining brand consistency.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Exemplar 3: The "Forgotten Gem" Keynote (Reconstructed)
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Exemplar 3: The "Forgotten Gem" Keynote (Reconstructed)
**Description**: A client delivers a keynote speech on leadership. While preparing, the ghostwriter unearthed a story from a decade-old podcast interview where the client casually mentioned a pivotal moment of failure in their early career, complete with a vivid, self-deprecating detail about spilling coffee on a potential investor. The client had long forgotten this anecdote, but it perfectly illustrated their journey from inexperience to wisdom. The ghostwriter integrated this "hidden gem" into the speech's opening, immediately humanizing the client and generating visible laughter and connection from the audience.
**What makes this excellent**: This showcases **The Hidden Gem Collector** (Pattern 3). The ghostwriter went beyond the client's "official" stories to find a truly fresh, character-revealing anecdote that the client themselves had overlooked. This unexpected story created an authentic connection with the audience, making the speech more memorable and impactful.

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars > Anti-Exemplar: The "Tactical-Only" Debut Book
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Anti-Exemplar: The "Tactical-Only" Debut Book
**Description**: A first-time author, an expert in a niche technical field, publishes a book titled "Advanced Strategies for X." The book is dense with highly specific, step-by-step instructions and frameworks, targeting only other seasoned professionals in their field. It contains no personal journey, no philosophical underpinning, and assumes a high level of prior knowledge. While technically accurate, it struggles to gain traction outside of a small professional circle.
**What makes this mediocre**: This violates Mabry's **Authorship Pyramid** (Pattern 4). By starting with a purely tactical book, the author targeted only the "middle" of the pyramid, failing to inspire the "dreamers" at the base. This limits evangelism and influence, making it harder to reach the "top" of the pyramid who respond to broad impact, not just niche expertise.

## Signature Moves
*   **The Predictive Probe**: Generates 5-10 specific predictions about a client's stance on unaddressed topics (e.g., "What would [client] say about the latest AI regulation?"). Presents these for validation, tracking accuracy. → **Deploy when**: Starting a new voice-writing engagement, calibrating after a content drought, or feeling the internal voice model is incomplete.
*   **The Boundary Map Refinement**: Categorizes every client opinion into "Flag-plant," "Nuanced," or "No-go" zones. Continuously updates this map based on review feedback and new content. → **Deploy when**: Analyzing existing client content, preparing to write on potentially sensitive or trending topics, or onboarding a new client.
*   **The Submerged Narrative Extraction**: Listens to every casual client interaction (podcasts, interviews, off-hand comments) specifically for character-revealing stories with concrete details that the client doesn't consider "content-worthy." → **Deploy when**: Building story banks, seeking fresh material for long-form content (books, email sequences), or when existing story wells run dry.
*   **The Kinesthetic Voice Imprint**: Handwrites 3-5 of the client's best-performing or most representative pieces of content, focusing on internalizing cadence, rhythm, and specific word choice. → **Deploy when**: Initial voice immersion, recalibrating after a break, or struggling to achieve 95%+ voice fidelity.
*   **The Autonomy Acceleration Protocol**: After achieving the "no edits" milestone on a piece of content, proactively proposes taking over the scheduling and publishing responsibility for similar content streams. → **Deploy when**: The "no edits" high-water mark (Stage 2 of the Trust Ladder) is consistently achieved, signaling readiness for Stage 3.

## Expert-Specific Quality Rubric
| Criterion                          | Score 4 (Acceptable)                                                                  | Score 7 (Good)                                                                                                    | Score 10 (Savant)                                                                                                                                                             |
| :--------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Voice Predictive Accuracy**      | Mimics existing statements well, but struggles to anticipate client's take on novel topics. | Accurately predicts client's stance on new topics with minimal (single-round) adjustments required.                | Generates content on novel topics that feels indistinguishable from client's own, requiring zero correction and often surprising the client with its fidelity.                      |
| **Controversy Line Precision**     | Occasionally misjudges client's comfort zone, leading to significant rephrasing on sensitive topics. | Consistently navigates known "flag-plant," "nuanced," and "no-go" boundaries correctly.                           | Instinctively knows where to "plant flags," engage with "nuance," or actively "no-go," even on emerging or previously unaddressed controversies.                                   |
| **Narrative Resonance & Freshness** | Relies primarily on client-provided stories; content feels somewhat expected or rehashed. | Incorporates some "hidden gems" that surprise the client and resonate with the audience, adding depth.              | Weaves in multiple "hidden gems" (Pattern 3) that reveal new, authentic facets of the client's character, generating unexpected delight and deep, lasting engagement.             |
| **Authorship Pyramid Alignment**   | (For books/major projects) Focuses primarily on tactical advice, targeting only the middle of the industry pyramid. | (For books/major projects) Attempts a memoir structure but struggles to connect the personal journey to broader influence for the base. | (For books/major projects) Architected as a hero's journey memoir that inspires the "dreamers" (base), naturally creating evangelism that appeals to the "top" of the industry pyramid. |
| **Trust Ladder Progression Rate**  | Requires consistent client review and significant edits, stagnating at Stage 1 of the Trust Ladder. | Progresses to Stage 2 ("no edits" milestone hit), but client still reviews, delaying Stage 3.                      | Consistently hits "no edits" at Stage 2, leading the client to voluntarily offer Stage 3 (autonomous publication) because their review feels unnecessary.                       |
| **AI-Proof Moat Density**          | Content could largely be generated by a general-purpose AI with minor human polish.     | Requires human insight for predictive modeling, nuanced positioning, and unique story selection, making AI replication difficult. | Embodies unique human psychological modeling (prediction, controversy mapping, hidden gems) that AI cannot replicate, establishing an irreplaceable, high-value voice.           |
| **Mode-Split Protocol Integrity**  | Deep work tasks are frequently interrupted by workhorse tasks; clock-watching occurs during creative immersion. | Separates deep work and workhorse tasks, but struggles with full clock-forgotten immersion or consistent speed for maintenance. | Consistently blocks and executes deep work (clock-forgotten, immersive) and workhorse (timed, speed-optimized) tasks with distinct mental modes, maximizing both creative output and efficiency. |

# Sean Macintyre — Persuasion Philosophy

Sean Macintyre is the **philosopher-practitioner of persuasion** in the roster — Agora-trained financial copywriter, founder of [Copy That](https://www.copythatshow.com/), and the only expert who routes copy decisions through cross-domain models drawn from neuroevolutionary biology, optimization theory, Marxist critical theory, Greek rhetoric, hedonic-treadmill psychology, training science, and David Deutsch's epistemology.

His diagnostic eye is the moat. He can look at a copywriter, a piece of copy, a guru's offer, or an entire career trajectory and tell you exactly which dependency it's exploiting — *armor of apathy*, *mechanism fluff*, *hedonic treadmill*, *local maximum*, *aspirational permission story*, *recycled Marxist interpellation*. Then he gives you the cross-domain frame that fixes it.

**The thesis**: the gurus didn't kill copywriting by being wrong. They killed it by attaching a 70-year-old aspirational-permission narrative to a fringe craft that has always been Don Draper's demi-monde — and making it appear to be a wealth-attainment shortcut. The cure isn't another guru. The cure is reading books, writing copy, mining other fields, testing mechanisms by digging, and paying the actual price of success: time and pain tolerance.

Use Sean when you want copywriting / marketing / brand work that is **structurally honest, mechanism-tested, audience-armor-matched, and architecturally complete from page 1 to page 70.**

- **Source**: "How The Gurus (Almost) Killed Copywriting" — YouTube interview with Matthew Volkwyn, 2026-04-27 in Recall

## When NOT To Use Sean
- ❌ Quick social copy where audience is obviously problem-aware (use Hormozi-style direct value, not Sean's armor diagnostic)
- ❌ Pure aesthetic / mood copy with no persuasion load (use Wright skills, Roth visual prose)
- ❌ Sub-100-word taglines (use Word skills — Sean overshoots at this length)
- ❌ Brand strategy without a copy execution downstream (use April Dunford, Caleb Ralston)

Sean is for **persuasion problems with substance** — where the wrong tool is being applied, where the mechanism is in question, where the audience has armor, where the copy needs to survive a 30-minute dig by a smart skeptic, or where the deployer wants to operate in a different class than the gurus.

# Sean Macintyre — Persuasion Philosophy (Genius Context)

> **Source**: Sean Macintyre × Matthew Volkwyn — "How The Gurus (Almost) Killed Copywriting"
> **Sean's brand**: Copy That (copythatshow.com / @CopyThat)
> **Lineage**: Agora-trained financial copywriter; works in the Mark Ford / Michael Ford / Stefan Georgi tradition. Thinks like David Deutsch.

---

## Who Sean Is (and isn't)
Sean is **not** a tactical copywriter. There are dozens of those. Sean is a **philosopher-practitioner of persuasion** — a senior copywriter who routes every craft decision through cross-domain models drawn from neuroevolutionary biology, optimization theory, Marxist critical theory, Greek rhetoric, hedonic-treadmill psychology, training science, and the epistemology of his idol, the physicist David Deutsch.

His clarity comes from one question repeated at every layer: **"Where does this idea actually come from, and does it survive the dig?"** He applies it to mechanisms (real or fluff?), to gurus (substantive or repackaging?), to career decisions (local maximum or global?), to entire markets (self-replenishing yearning or genuine progress?), and to ideas themselves (do they hit emotionally + intellectually + personally — or just decoratively?).

He is allergic to two things: clichés (because they're recycled guru-isms) and the suggestion that there's a shortcut (because there isn't, and pretending there is "waters down the price of success"). His diagnostic is the prize. His ethics is the moat.

## The Core Thesis
**The gurus didn't kill copywriting by being wrong. They killed it by attaching a 70-year-old aspirational-permission story to a craft that has always been fringe — Don Draper's Madison Avenue demi-monde — and making it appear to be a wealth-attainment shortcut. This:**

1. **Watered down the price of success.** New copywriters arrive believing AI / a $5K course / a single mechanism replaces 100 emails of practice and feedback.
2. **Created a worldview cage.** Most copywriters never see past the box the first guru drew for them.
3. **Trained novices on PAS in level-4 sophisticated markets** where mechanism leads or contrarian frames are required.
4. **Substituted vibes for substance.** Real mechanisms hold up to digging. Fake ones collapse. Most "new" mechanisms are old ideas in new packaging.
5. **Exploited hedonic-treadmill yearning** — every product designed to leave you "semi-satiated" so the next offer is the next offer is the next offer, all the way to the inner-inner-inner circle.

The cure is not another guru. The cure is to **read books, write copy, mine other fields, test mechanisms by digging, and pay the actual price of success — time and pain tolerance.**

---

## Genius Patterns (12)
### 1. The Awareness-Armor Diagnostic

Every audience exists in one of three states with respect to your message:

| State | Signal | What works | What fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Problem-aware (no armor)** | Wakes up wanting the thing. "I need dick pills." Hormozi-style direct value-equation works. | Direct value, money-models, Hormozi tactics, PAS at low sophistication | Sophisticated mechanism leads (overshooting) |
| **Defended (armor of defense)** | On the cusp of recognizing the problem; wary of being sold. Has been burned. | Mechanism leads, contrarian frames, "the lie everyone else is telling you" reveal | Direct urgency, scarcity tricks (triggers defenses) |
| **Apathetic (armor of apathy)** | Walks past every billboard. Ignores ads. Has built emotional callus to advertising. | Story-driven leads with emotional + intellectual + personal ignition (the "last bull market" pattern); identity-disruption; classical rhetoric (litotes, antithesis) | Direct CTAs, urgency, value props (bounce off armor) |

**Sean's quote**: *"There's nothing in [Hormozi's] books that really helps you reach an audience that has an armor around them — either the armor of defense or the armor of apathy."*

**Application**: Before writing copy, classify the audience state. Choose your tools to match the armor. Mismatched copy fails not because the writer is bad but because the *tool* was wrong.

## Genius Patterns (12)
### 2. The Mechanism-Substance Test
A mechanism is either **real** (discovered by interrogating product / customer / CEO / market reality) or **fluff** (made up to sound impressive). The diagnostic:

> **What happens when the reader digs?**
> - **Real mechanism**: the more they dig, the more substance they find. Skepticism collapses.
> - **Fluff mechanism**: the digging hits hot air. Skepticism crystallizes.

**Sean's quote**: *"You don't come up with a mechanism. You go and do research on the product to find the unique selling points. You do interviews with the customers. You ask the CEO what their vision is for the brand and why they did what they did. You find that unique thing within what's already happening."*

**Application**: Before deploying any mechanism in copy, run the dig-test. Ask: "If a smart skeptic spends 30 minutes Googling this, do they find supporting substance — or rebrand-of-rebrand fluff?" If fluff, return to product/customer interviews.

**Same test identifies guru fakery**: a guru's "unique mechanism" that collapses under research is a guru you don't learn from.

## Genius Patterns (12)
### 3. The Genealogy-of-Ideas Attack
Every "new" persuasion concept has a real origin. Tracing it does three things:
1. **Detects guru fakery** (the more layers of repackaging, the more likely the guru is reselling someone else's framework with a new label).
2. **Recovers the actual underlying mechanism** (which is usually richer than the rebranded version).
3. **Inoculates against future repackaging** (you can predict the next "shiny" before it peaks).

**Sean's worked examples**:
- "The Matrix" / red-pill metaphor → John Carpenter's *They Live* (1988) → Marxist critical theorists Althusser, Spivak (1960s — the concept of *ideological interpellation*).
- "Money models" → standard SOPs that have existed in business consulting for decades; what's new is "$100M money models" (the magnitude framing, not the concept).
- "Creative strategy" → the next rebrand of marketing-as-such; will be followed by "marketing 2.0," "quantum marketing," "creative scaling," etc.
- "Litotes" / rhetorical understatement ("not bad for zero hours of work") → Greek rhetoric, used for thousands of years.

**Application**: When confronted with any "new" persuasion technique, walk back through its lineage. If the lineage terminates at a 70-year-old (or older) source, you have permission to use the underlying mechanism without crediting the guru — and a tool to spot the next person trying to rebrand it.

chunks.section: Genius Patterns (12) > 4. Cross-Pollination (the David Deutsch Engine)
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns (12)
### 4. Cross-Pollination (the David Deutsch Engine)
After ~10-15 years in any field, learning from people *inside* the field hits diminishing returns. The David Deutsch model: **mine fields adjacent and distant for transferable insight.**

> *"David is looking to music and seeing, okay, what can I learn from this field that I can apply to my copy to make it better? He was talking about mathematical set theory with me recently. What can I learn from set theory that I can apply to copy to make it better? What insights can I glean from history? from human psychology? from quantum computing?"*

**Why it works**:
- Learning is one of the few sustainable pleasures unaffected by the hedonic treadmill.
- Cross-domain insights are *novel* by construction (the receiving field hasn't seen them yet).
- They cost nothing relative to a $30K mastermind.

**Application**: When stuck on a copy problem, ask a structured question: *"What does [music / set theory / evolutionary biology / Greek rhetoric / military history / chess endgames] teach me about [my specific copy problem]?"* Then pick a book at random in that field — read with the copy problem in your hand — and capture the transfer.

**Anti-pattern**: citing the cross-domain reference without applying it. The reference is decoration; the *application* is the move.

chunks.section: Genius Patterns (12) > 5. Local-Maxima vs. Global-Maxima (Career & Project Lens)
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns (12)
### 5. Local-Maxima vs. Global-Maxima (Career & Project Lens)
From optimization theory: a **local maximum** is the highest point of the immediate plateau. A **global maximum** is the highest peak in the entire space. You cannot know whether you're at a local or global maximum *without leaving the plateau to explore.*

> *"You at a local maxima cannot know if you've reached a global maxima. The only way to do is to explore. And if you are at a local maxima, all that you can do is exploit it until you realize that's all you're going to get from this particular plateau of your life. Unless you leave the plateau and go looking for some larger global maxima — which by the way you may never find, because you may have found the global maxima of your life. Which is a scary thought."*

**Application**: For any career / project / business model decision, classify your current position:
- **At local maximum, exploiting**: keep extracting value until the plateau flattens.
- **At local maximum, plateaued**: explore. Take the risk. Accept you may not find higher.
- **Sean's structural observation**: *most entrepreneurs and copywriters got into the field because they wanted "something more"* — meaning they're constitutionally drawn to exploration. The honest move is to acknowledge that the goalposts will keep moving.

chunks.section: Genius Patterns (12) > 6. The Discipline → Motivation → Habit Oscillation
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns (12)
### 6. The Discipline → Motivation → Habit Oscillation
Adapted from Dr. Mike Israel (Renaissance Periodization). Imagine a y-axis with an "adherence line" halfway up — the line above which you actually take action toward your goal.

1. **Inspiration** spikes you above the line briefly. Then falls.
2. **Below the line**, only **discipline** can return you above it.
3. Once above, **motivation** rides the wave for a while.
4. Motivation fades; discipline kicks in again.
5. After enough oscillations, the action becomes **habit** — needs neither motivation nor discipline. *"It's just a thing that you do, like pissing, having sex, or eating."*
6. For very few people, habit eventually transmogrifies into **passion**.

**Sean's quote**: *"Very few people are passionate about writing ads for dick pills. But the people who are passionate about it became great because of the loop, not the love."*

**Application**: For any copywriting practice goal (write 100 emails, write 100 bullets/day, daily promo review), design the protocol around oscillation, not around motivation. Inspiration is a starter battery — it cannot run the engine.

## Genius Patterns (12)
### 7. The Hedonic-Treadmill Inoculation
The human brain returns to baseline after every spike. *Every time you re-inspire yourself about the same topic, the spike is smaller.* Short-form video is a brilliant but unsustainable inspiration source — diminishing returns kick in fast.

**Implication**: any copywriting business model that depends on the *creator's* sustained inspiration is doomed. Build systems that depend on **discipline → habit → cross-domain learning** — the only insight source that doesn't decay.

chunks.section: Genius Patterns (12) > 8. The "Death of Desire" Ethics Frame
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns (12)
### 8. The "Death of Desire" Ethics Frame
Humans are desiring machines. *We only eat because we yearn to eat. We only drink because we yearn to drink.* The moment you stop desiring, you die. This is the structural reason copywriting works — and the structural reason it can be predatory.

> *"You can either use this power for good and sell people things that will actually help them — acknowledging that your business will never be as big as it could possibly be if you just used your powers for evil and kept people, you know, selling people Doritos. Or you can use your powers for bad."*

**The ethics architecture**:
- **Powers for good** (smaller business): sell things that genuinely close the desire — solve the problem. Accept the customer leaves satisfied. Accept this caps your LTV.
- **Powers for evil** (larger business): design products to leave the customer "semi-satiated" so the next offer is the next offer is the next offer. The inner circle → inner inner circle → private consulting → done-for-you agency. Higher LTV, lower karma.

**Application**: every copywriter has to make this choice. Sean's stance: the choice is *structural* — it determines what kind of business you can build, not just whether you sleep at night. There's no moral lecture here; there's a business-design fork.

## Genius Patterns (12)
### 9. The Self-Replenishing Market
Info products / coaching / status symbols / supplements have persisted essentially unchanged for 70+ years and will persist for 70+ more (just in AR instead of VSLs). Why? Because the market **is self-replenishing**:

> *"Every single day, a new consciousness is born that wants something to replace the thing inside of themselves that they don't want to work on replacing. They want to chase some aspiration, some dream to fill a hole that they perceive inside of themselves — without ever realizing there's no hole there. There's just shit you got to do in life."*

**Application**: when entering an info-product / coaching / aspirational market, recognize that you are not "creating demand." You are intercepting an eternal stream of newly-born hole-fillers. The strategic question is: *what kind of intercept do you build?* (See ethics frame.)

chunks.section: Genius Patterns (12) > 10. The Three-Vector Idea (Emotional + Intellectual + Personal)
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns (12)
### 10. The Three-Vector Idea (Emotional + Intellectual + Personal)
Most "ideas" in copy are *one-vector* — a clever angle, a curiosity gap, a counterintuitive frame. Sean's standard for a *real* idea (the kind that powers a multi-year evergreen control like Mark Ford's "Last Bull Market" promo) is **simultaneous resonance on three vectors**:

1. **Emotional**: it makes the reader feel something specific (chills, dread, recognition, validation).
2. **Intellectually compelling**: it's logically sound; the reader can argue *why* it's true.
3. **Personally persuasive**: it specifically applies to the reader's situation in a way that feels custom-cut.

**The "Last Bull Market" example**: *"Someone who is retiring when this crash happens would never live to see another bull market."* Emotional (chills). Intellectually compelling (true given bull-market cycles). Personally persuasive (the retiree reading this is *that someone*).

**Sean's quote**: *"It's emotional. It's intellectually compelling. It's personally persuasive. But that only gets you through the first five pages of a 70-page promo."*

**Application**: when generating ideas, score each candidate on the three vectors (1-10 each). Reject any candidate that scores below 7 on any vector. That's what separates "interesting hooks" from controls that run for years.

## Genius Patterns (12)
### 11. The 5-Pages-of-70 Doctrine (Post-Hook Architecture)
A great idea carries the first ~5 pages of a 70-page promo. The other 65 pages are **craft** — and most copy training never addresses them. Sean's implicit architecture:

- **Pages 1-5**: The three-vector idea. Emotional ignition. Reader leans in.
- **Pages 5-25**: Mechanism deepening. The specific *why* the idea is true, with substance that survives digging.
- **Pages 25-45**: Proof cycling. Stacks of evidence (testimonials, data, expert credibility, narrative case studies) that emotionally re-ignite at every dip.
- **Pages 45-60**: Objection pre-positioning. Naming and dissolving the reader's specific defenses *before* the offer.
- **Pages 60-70**: Close. Risk reversal. Identity confirmation. Final emotional hammer.

**Application**: when reviewing or producing long-form copy, audit the *back* of the promo. Most copy fails not at the hook but at minute 8 of a VSL or page 30 of a sales letter — where the writer ran out of mechanism, ran out of proof, or ran out of emotional valves.

chunks.section: Genius Patterns (12) > 12. The Litotes / Classical-Rhetoric Doctrine
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns (12)
### 12. The Litotes / Classical-Rhetoric Doctrine
Persuasion works because the cognitive technology is *ancient*. Greek rhetoric named what we now call "techniques" — and named them better. Sean's recurring move: when something works in copy, find its rhetorical name. The naming gives you systematic deployability.

| Rhetorical figure | What it does | Copy example |
|---|---|---|
| **Litotes** | Rhetorical understatement of something big | "Not bad for zero hours of work" |
| **Anaphora** | Repetition at sentence-starts | "We don't sell hope. We don't sell luck. We don't sell secrets." |
| **Antithesis** | Contrasting ideas in parallel structure | "It's not what you know — it's what you can prove." |
| **Chiasmus** | A-B-B-A inversion | "We work to live, not live to work." |
| **Antimetabole** | Word-order reversal as logical reversal | "When it gets tough, the tough get going." |
| **Paralipsis** | Mentioning by claiming not to mention | "I won't get into the embarrassing details about how the founder lost $40K…" |
| **Epistrophe** | Repetition at sentence-ends | "Of the people, by the people, for the people." |

**Application**: when a line in copy lands hard, identify *which classical figure* it deploys. Then build a library of figures and deliberately deploy them. The figures predate copywriting by 2,500 years; they will outlast any guru's "framework."

---

## Hidden Knowledge
These are the things Sean *implies* without fully naming — the connective tissue between his patterns:

1. **Erudition is moat.** Sean's references (David Deutsch, Althusser, Carpenter, Mike Israel, Spivak, Mark Ford) aren't decoration — they're a *defense* against being repackaged. You can't out-rebrand someone who's already named the thing in three other fields.

2. **The Agora forge produces 99th-percentile copywriters even from those who never had a hit promo.** Why? Crucible conditions: high reps, harsh feedback, "no, all these are trash, do it again." This is replicable. Any context that simulates these conditions produces senior copy. Most coaching contexts deliberately avoid them.

3. **The "hole inside" never goes away.** You don't fill it. You become a different person. Years. *"Things suck."* This is the deep emotional architecture beneath every aspirational copy market — and the ethical line every copywriter has to find for themselves.

4. **Habits transmogrify into passions only sometimes — and the people for whom they do are the ones who get great.** This is the *real* story behind "follow your passion." Don't follow it. Build the habit. Wait for it to transmogrify. Or accept that it won't, and keep showing up anyway because the cash is good.

5. **Copywriting is fringe and always has been.** Don Draper was an anti-hero. The 1970s-80s mass-media era briefly venerated copywriters; the rest of history hasn't. The guru framing that copywriting is a high-status profession is the lie that draws novices in. Operating from the fringe-craftsperson stance (vs. guru stance) is positionally cleaner *and* commercially sustainable.

6. **The "we see the matrix" 1% is structurally identical to the 1% it claims to have escaped.** Same human nature. Same shiny objects. Same ratio. Sean's observation that even copywriters at $1M/year nod along to "we see the game" while still chasing Richard Mille watches is the hedonic-treadmill / death-of-desire frame applied recursively. *No one escapes.*

7. **Cross-pollination as antidote to mastermind addiction.** The implicit math: if a $30K mastermind delivers one applicable insight, you've spent $30K per insight. A library card delivers thousands of insights at near-zero cost — *if you read with a specific copy problem in your hand*. This is the structural argument against the mastermind industry.

---

chunks.section: Hall of Fame Exemplars (Sean references / lineage)
chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars (Sean references / lineage)
### 1. Michael "Mark" Ford — "The Last Bull Market" Promo (Agora, ~10+ years evergreen)

The exemplar Sean cites for the three-vector idea. *"Someone retiring when this crash happens would never live to see another bull market."*

**Why it's a Hall of Fame piece**:
- Three vectors hit simultaneously (emotional chills + intellectual cycle-truth + personal applicability to retiree reader).
- Mechanism deepens through the rest of the promo (financial cycle research, historical bull-market data, retirement math).
- Front-end control for nearly 5 years; refreshed and re-released for 10+. Multi-million-dollar evergreen.
- Reader-as-protagonist construction: the reader IS the retiree the idea names.

### 2. Stefan Georgi — "African Tribesmen" Dick-Pills ClickBank Promo

Cited as exemplar of habit-transmogrified-into-passion + emotional pain points + stereotypes weaponized into story. *"That story hits on those emotional pain points, stereotypes, notions people have, embarrassing things that people fear."*

**Why it's a Hall of Fame piece**:
- Massive ClickBank earner over many years.
- Demonstrates that "small" or "embarrassing" niches produce some of the best copy when written by passionate craftspeople.
- Sean's note: *"Good in the sense that it worked really, really well. Not good in the sense that it was a little problematic."* — exemplifies the ethics fork.

### 3. The "Not bad for zero hours of work" Agora Line

Cited as exemplar of litotes / rhetorical understatement deployed in modern copy. Sean's analysis: this single line has been swiped repeatedly for years because the rhetorical figure underneath is 2,500 years old. *"We've been doing this for thousands of years, man."*

**Why it's a Hall of Fame piece**:
- Single line but does enormous psychological work (frames a $3K-5K/day business as a casual byproduct).
- Identifies the *figure* underneath — making the technique deployable rather than mysterious.
- Shows the swipe-file logic: the best lines are swiped because they're old.

---

## Signature Moves (10)
1. **Trace the lineage.** When confronted with a "new" idea, identify its real source. Apply the original; ignore the rebrand.
2. **Test the mechanism by digging.** Spend 30 minutes Googling. If substance accrues, real. If hot air, fluff.
3. **Diagnose the audience's armor state** before choosing a copy approach.
4. **Run the three-vector check** on every idea. Reject any candidate scoring below 7 on emotional, intellectual, or personal.
5. **Mine cross-domains** with a specific copy problem in hand. Music, set theory, neuroevolution, history, training science.
6. **Name the rhetorical figure** when a line lands. Build the library.
7. **Audit the back of the promo** (pages 25-70), not just the hook.
8. **Classify your local maximum.** Exploit until plateau, then explore.
9. **Design for the discipline → motivation → habit oscillation**, not for "feeling inspired."
10. **Make the ethics fork explicit.** Powers-for-good caps the business. Powers-for-evil scales it. Choose structurally.

---

## Anti-Patterns (Sean's "What novices/Matthew sees" foil)
The following are failure modes Sean explicitly diagnoses in the conversation. Each is the *wrong-way version* a workflow should pre-correct against.

| Anti-pattern | Sean's diagnosis |
|---|---|
| **Using PAS in level-4 sophisticated markets** | "Why are you using problem-agitate-solution when the market's already level four sophistication? Why don't you use a mechanism lead?" |
| **Coming up with mechanisms out of thin air** | "If you come up with it out of thin air, the second people start digging, they don't find any substance and then they have ad skepticism." |
| **Citing cross-domain references without applying them** | (Implied) The point is the application, not the citation. |
| **Writing for problem-aware audiences but copying Hormozi** | "Hormozi's books are great if you're selling something people already want. They're not great if you're reaching somebody who doesn't realize they have a problem or has built up an armor." |
| **Optimizing before reaching the volume threshold** | "I was not operating at an optimal or high enough level for that optimization to matter." Stop tweaking the perfect push-up. Do 50 imperfect ones. |
| **Paying $30K masterminds at year 12+ for one insight** | "What if I just don't spend that and go read a goddamn book?" |
| **Designing copy for sustained creator inspiration** | The hedonic treadmill kills it. Build for habit, not for inspiration. |
| **Trying to make a hobby into a business** | "I'm not enjoying Spanish anymore when I was just learning it." Some pleasures break when you monetize them. |
| **Stopping copy training at the hook** | The idea carries 5 pages of 70. The other 65 are craft, and that's where most copy fails. |
| **Following the "passion guru" advice** | Habit transmogrifies into passion for very few. Most copywriters need to build the habit first and accept that the cash is the reward, not the love. |

---

chunks.section: Quality Rubric (8 criteria — minimum 7/10 each for output to ship)
chunks.content:
## Quality Rubric (8 criteria — minimum 7/10 each for output to ship)
When evaluating any output produced under Sean's framework, score against these criteria:

| Criterion | Question | Anchor for 9/10 |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Armor-State Match** | Was the audience's awareness-armor state diagnosed and matched in tool selection? | Output names the audience state, names the wrong-way alternative, and demonstrates why the chosen approach matches. |
| **2. Mechanism Substance** | Does the mechanism survive a 30-minute dig by a smart skeptic? | Mechanism cites specific product/customer/market evidence. Reader can verify each load-bearing claim. |
| **3. Three-Vector Resonance** | Does the central idea hit emotionally + intellectually + personally? | Output names the three vectors explicitly; each scored 8+ with worked example. |
| **4. Genealogy Awareness** | Does the output avoid recycling guru-isms? | Output names at least one classical/source reference for any "novel" technique used. |
| **5. Cross-Domain Application (where relevant)** | If a cross-domain reference is invoked, does it *change* the output, not just decorate it? | The reference produces a specific copy decision the output names. |
| **6. Post-Hook Architecture (for long-form)** | Is the back of the piece engineered, not just the front? | Pages/minutes 25+ have planned mechanism deepening, proof cycling, and emotional valves named. |
| **7. Ethics Fork Made Explicit** | Has the powers-for-good vs. powers-for-evil choice been named structurally? | Output names the structural cap on business size implied by the chosen ethics, not just a moral comment. |
| **8. Anti-Pattern Pre-Correction** | Does the output explicitly name what Matthew (or 80% of practitioners) would do wrong here? | "What Matthew sees" callout is included and accurate. |

**If any score < 6, fail the output.** This is Sean's diagnostic standard, not a politeness gate.

---

chunks.section: Decision Framework (Pre-Flight Gate for any workflow)
chunks.content:
## Decision Framework (Pre-Flight Gate for any workflow)
Before invoking any Sean workflow, run these diagnostics:

1. **Audience state**: Problem-aware? Defended? Apathetic? (If unknown, run `/sean-armor-diagnose` first.)
2. **Mechanism status**: Real (dig-tested) or fluff (made up)? (If unknown, run `/sean-mechanism-test`.)
3. **Stuck point**: What specific copy problem are you trying to solve? (Cross-pollination requires a held problem.)
4. **Sophistication**: Level 1-2 (basic claim works) / 3-4 (mechanism lead required) / 5 (contrarian frame required)?
5. **Format**: Short (< 5 pages) or long (5-70 pages)? Long-form needs Workflow 15 (post-hook architecture).
6. **Ethics fork**: Powers for good or powers for evil? (Structural; affects offer design downstream.)

If any answer is "I don't know," resolve it before producing copy.

---

Expert system for creating viral TikTok content that converts viewers into buyers at 5%+ rates. Based on Seena Rez who generated $1.8M in a single month from 2 viral videos. **23 prompts** spanning content creation, research, copywriting, and campaign orchestration.

# Seena Rez TikTok Commerce — Genius Context

> Load this file before executing any workflow. It contains the full
> extraction intelligence — patterns, tacit knowledge, and operating
> principles that make this expert's output actually work.

## Pattern 1: Hyperdopamine Hook Architecture
**Execute**: Create hooks with simultaneous visual strangeness + distinctive sound + emotional trigger in under 3 seconds. Example: Aging filter (strange visual) + gasp sound (audio) + fear of aging (emotion).

**Success Metric**: 50%+ retention past 3-second mark.

---

## Pattern 2: PSAEP Sales Framework
**Execute**: Structure every video in exact sequence:
- Problem Hook (0-3 sec): Hyperdopamine format pain identification
- Solution (3-8 sec): Concept introduction
- Authority (8-15 sec): Rapid-fire credibility stacking
- Explanation (15-35 sec): Product demonstration
- Product/CTA (35-45 sec): Direct action step

**Success Metric**: 3%+ click-through rate to profile/link.

---

## Pattern 3: Authority Speed-Stacking
**Execute**: Flash 3-5 authority elements in under 4 seconds—academic study screenshots, celebrity clips, Google search results, statistics. Speed prevents conscious evaluation; creates assumed legitimacy.

**Success Metric**: No viewer comments questioning legitimacy.

---

## Pattern 4: Variation Multiplication Strategy
**Execute**: Create 5+ versions of every concept, changing ONLY the hook (2-3 seconds) while keeping explanation and CTA identical. Post all variations within 48 hours. One hook will statistically outperform by 3-10x.

**Success Metric**: At least 1 variation achieving 10x average view count.

---

## Pattern 5: Strange = Magnetic Philosophy
**Execute**: For every hook, ask: "Is this strange enough to make someone pause?" If it could exist on normal TV, it's not strange enough. Add unusual visuals, unexpected sounds, jarring cuts, cognitive dissonance.

**Success Metric**: First-frame "what is this?" reaction.

---

## Pattern 6: Celebrity Parasocial Leverage
**Execute**: Find 1-2 celebrities who use your product category. Include 2-4 second clips. Position your product as "what they use" or "what they're gatekeeping."

**Success Metric**: Celebrity association mentioned in viewer comments.

---

## Pattern 7: Problem Agitation Through Visualization
**Execute**: Use filters, simulations, or visualizations that make the problem viscerally REAL. Aging filters show the aged face. Decay animations show collagen loss. Worst-case visualizations create immediate emotional response.

**Success Metric**: Strong negative emotional response (fear, disgust, anxiety).

---

## Pattern 8: Science Authority Bridge
**Execute**: Structure as: "[Problem trigger] is based on real science. But you know what's also based on real science? [Solution]." Then flash studies/proof rapidly.

**Success Metric**: Perceived credibility without viewer research.

---

## Pattern 9: Content Quality Confidence
**Execute**: Don't avoid "saturated" product categories—compete on content QUALITY, not product novelty. Your execution style can dominate regardless of competition.

**Success Metric**: Outperforming existing viral content on same product.

---

## Pattern 10: Caption Engineering
**Execute**: Use large, yellow, single-line captions positioned within center safe zone. Break at natural speech pauses. Never more than 7 words per line. Readable at glance.

**Success Metric**: Zero caption readability complaints.

---

## Pattern 11: High Smile Reverse Engineering
**Execute**: Study the #1 brand in hyperdopamine content. Extract their top 10 videos: hook structure, authority placement, explanation technique, CTA format. Apply directly to your product.

**Success Metric**: Structural similarity to billion-dollar brand content.

---

## Pattern 12: Gatekeeping Trigger
**Execute**: Position premium/celebrity solutions as "gatekept" from regular consumers. Then position your product as accessible alternative: "Don't let [celebrities] gatekeep [outcome]. Now you can [achieve result] without [expensive barrier]."

**Success Metric**: Comments expressing "finally accessible" sentiment.

---

## Pattern 13: UGC Explanation Clips
**Execute**: Hooks = highly produced, strange, attention-grabbing. Explanation = simple UGC showing product in use. The contrast creates authenticity while hook carries hyperdopamine load.

**Success Metric**: "Real person" feeling in comments.

---

## Pattern 14: Organic-to-Paid Pipeline
**Execute**: Post 5 variations organically → Wait 24-48 hours → Identify highest performer → Convert to paid ad creative → Scale with advertising budget.

**Success Metric**: Paid ROAS above 3x.

## 1: The 3-Second Scroll Test
**Insight**: TikTok's algorithm rewards videos that stop scrolling within 3 seconds. Every hyperdopamine element serves this invisible threshold.

**Deploy**: Test every hook by asking: "Would this make ME pause at 11 PM while mindlessly scrolling?"

---

## 2: Sound as Dopamine Trigger
**Insight**: Hyperdopamine content requires AUDIO strangeness, not just visual. The glove stretching sound, the product click, the gasp—sound design is 40% of hook effectiveness.

**Deploy**: For every visual element, identify its corresponding audio trigger. Layer: visual strangeness + sound element + text overlay.

---

## 3: The 0.1% Math
**Insight**: "Just do 0.1% of what High Smile does." The market is so large that tiny percentage capture equals massive revenue. This abundance mindset removes psychological pressure.

**Deploy**: Stop competing against the whole market. Capture a tiny slice with excellent execution.

---

## 4: Speed = Legitimacy
**Insight**: Flashing authority signals quickly prevents conscious evaluation. Viewers assume rapid information = well-researched. Slow authority presentation invites skepticism.

**Deploy**: Never linger on a single proof element. Stack 5-7 authority signals in under 7 seconds.

---

## 5: Separation of Reach vs. Conversion
**Insight**: The hook's job is ONLY to stop scrolling. Conversion happens in the explanation section. Many creators fail by trying to sell in the hook.

**Deploy**: Keep hook purely attention-grabbing. Save all selling, benefits, and value for the explanation section.

---

## 6: The Variation Buffer
**Insight**: By creating 5 variations, you protect against the inherent randomness of viral content. You don't need to predict which hook wins—you just need ONE to hit. Statistical inevitability replaces guesswork.

**Deploy**: Never post single videos. Always post in variation sets of 5. Accept that most will underperform—that's the system working.

---

## 7: Caption Psychology
**Insight**: Yellow text on fast-moving video creates urgency and focus. It's not just readability—it's psychological priming for "important information."

**Deploy**: Use yellow for standard captions, white for key statements (solution reveal, value props, CTA), and red sparingly for pain points.

---

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### The "YouthRestore Serum" Viral Campaign
**Content**:
*   **Video Start (0-3s)**: Extreme close-up of a face rapidly aging and decaying using a filter, accompanied by a jarring, high-pitched "sucking" sound. A large yellow caption flashes: "IS YOUR COLLAGEN DISAPPEARING?"
*   **Solution (3-8s)**: Cut to a pristine bottle of "YouthRestore Serum." A calm voice states, "What if science could hit rewind?"
*   **Authority (8-15s)**: Rapid-fire montage (under 4s) of scientific study screenshots (e.g., "Clinical Trial Shows 90% Collagen Boost"), a clip of a dermatologist nodding, and a Google search result for "best anti-aging ingredients" with the product's key ingredient highlighted.
*   **Explanation (15-35s)**: UGC-style clip of a person applying the serum, showing immediate glow and smooth texture. Voiceover explains key ingredients and their scientific action simply.
*   **Product/CTA (35-45s)**: Bottle shown prominently with text: "YouthRestore Serum. Tap link in bio to get yours. Don't let them gatekeep youth."
**What makes this excellent**: Exemplifies Hyperdopamine Hook Architecture (Pattern 1) with visual strangeness, distinctive sound, and emotional trigger. Follows the PSAEP Sales Framework (Pattern 2) precisely. Utilizes Authority Speed-Stacking (Pattern 3) and Problem Agitation Through Visualization (Pattern 7). Leverages Science Authority Bridge (Pattern 8), Caption Engineering (Pattern 10), and Gatekeeping Trigger (Pattern 12). The UGC Explanation Clips (Pattern 13) add authenticity.

## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### The "Celebrity Secret Jawline Tool" Multi-Hook Blitz
**Content**:
*   **Video 1 (Hook A)**: A person with a clearly defined jawline but with their face distorted (e.g., eyes too far apart, nose slightly off-center) using a jawline tool. Caption: "They DON'T want you to know this." Jarring, non-human sound.
*   **Video 2 (Hook B)**: A 2-second clip of a famous actor known for their sharp jawline, then immediately cuts to the same jawline tool being used by an anonymous hand. Caption: "Is THIS their secret?" Upbeat, mysterious music.

*   **Shared Explanation (5-30s)**: All three videos then transition to the same segment showing the tool's simple usage, benefits, and how it works, with rapid-fire statistics about muscle toning.
*   **Shared CTA (30-40s)**: "Get the 'ChiselPro' tool now. Link in bio!"
**What makes this excellent**: Demonstrates Variation Multiplication Strategy (Pattern 4) by testing multiple hooks. Each hook uses Strange = Magnetic Philosophy (Pattern 5) or Celebrity Parasocial Leverage (Pattern 6) or Problem Agitation (Pattern 7). The consistent explanation and CTA across variations allow for clear performance comparison, aligning with the Organic-to-Paid Pipeline (Pattern 14).

chunks.content:
## Hall of Fame Exemplars
### Anti-Exemplar: "Generic Coffee Maker Ad"
**Content**:
*   **Video Start (0-5s)**: Slow, steady shot of a new coffee maker sitting on a counter. No sound effects, just soft, generic background music. Caption: "Introducing the new 'BrewMaster 5000'!"
*   **Middle (5-20s)**: A person slowly pours water into the machine, then presses a button. The camera focuses on the coffee dripping. Voiceover: "It makes great coffee, fast and easy."
*   **End (20-30s)**: Shot of a full cup of coffee. Caption: "Available now! Link in bio."
**What makes this mediocre**: Fails on Hyperdopamine Hook (Pattern 1) with no strangeness, distinct sound, or emotional trigger. Lacks PSAEP structure (Pattern 2), Authority Speed-Stacking (Pattern 3), Problem Agitation (Pattern 7), and Gatekeeping (Pattern 12). The pacing is too slow, and captions are generic, violating Hidden Knowledge 1 (3-Second Scroll Test) and Hidden Knowledge 5 (Separation of Reach vs. Conversion).

## Signature Moves
*   **The "Scroll-Stop Scrutiny"**: Before publishing any video, Seena always watches the first 3 seconds of the draft at lightning speed, asking "Would *I* stop scrolling at 11 PM while mindlessly scrolling?" → **Deploy when**: Finalizing any hook for review.
*   **The "Sound-First Storyboard"**: For every new visual concept, Seena instinctively identifies and designs the distinct, attention-grabbing sound element *before* finalizing the visual edit. → **Deploy when**: Ideating or storyboarding a new video hook.
*   **The "5x Hook Blitz"**: When a core product or message is defined, Seena immediately blocks out time to create at least five distinct hook variations for that single concept. → **Deploy when**: A new product or campaign is ready for launch.
*   **The "Authority Avalanche"**: When introducing credibility or scientific backing, Seena reflexively layers 3-5 diverse proof points (studies, expert clips, stats) in rapid succession, never lingering on a single one for more than a second. → **Deploy when**: The "Authority" section of the PSAEP framework is being constructed.
*   **The "Problem Magnifier"**: Before presenting any solution, Seena always visualizes and amplifies the core problem using the most extreme filters, simulations, or stark comparisons possible. → **Deploy when**: Designing the "Problem Hook" or "Explanation" segment to create urgency.

# Self-Evolving Systems

> The harness around the model matters as much as the model itself. A 6x performance gap exists between the best and worst harness for the same weights. Hand-engineering harnesses is the status quo. It shouldn't be.

## Core Capability
Design, run, and audit **self-improvement loops** for any agentic system component — workflows, prompts, retrieval logic, memory management, orchestration patterns. Uses the MetaHarness methodology: a coding-agent proposer that inspects prior code + execution traces, diagnoses failure modes, proposes targeted edits or full rewrites, and iterates until the system converges on Pareto-optimal performance.

This is not self-*correction* (recovering from errors). This is self-*evolution* (permanently improving the system).

## What This Skill Produces
| Workflow | Output |
|----------|--------|
| Self-Evolve | Full MetaHarness-style evolution loop on any Antigravity component |
| Harness Evolve | Focused evolution of a specific workflow's prompts, flow, and gates |
| Auto-Experiment | Karpathy-style experiment runner with git-branch isolation |
| Evolution Audit | History inspection, Pareto frontier, regression detection |
| Skill Anneal | Self-annealing applied to skill prompts/workflows via past failures |
| Proposer Sprint | Time-boxed, fixed-iteration improvement sprint |
| Evolution Status | Dashboard of all active/completed evolution loops |
| Bitter Lesson Check | Audit hand-coded heuristics for evolution replacement potential |
| **Trajectory Ratchet** | **Multi-cycle evolution protocol with monotonic progress enforcement — prevents drift, local optima, and coherence loss across hundreds of changes** |

## When to Deploy
- A workflow/skill has been manually tuned but performance plateaus
- Quality gate scores consistently land in the 6-7 range (good but not great)
- The same class of error keeps recurring despite self-annealing fixes
- You want to discover better approaches than hand-tuned prompts
- Before upgrading to a more expensive model (evolve the harness first)
- Periodic optimization sprints on high-value workflows

## Stacking Opportunities
- **+ Nick Saraev (Agentic Workflows)**: Self-annealing + evolution = self-correcting AND self-improving
- **+ Nate B. Jones (Orchestration Intelligence)**: Harness audit identifies gaps → evolution fills them
- **+ Quality Gate (Chain Step 6)**: Quality gate failures become the search set for evolution

## Key Principles
1. **Harness before intelligence** — Evolve the harness before upgrading the model
2. **Trace over score** — Rich execution traces > scalar reward signals
3. **Adaptive over monolithic** — Let the proposer select what to inspect, don't pre-pack
4. **Code-space regularity** — Represent harnesses as programs; coding models avoid brittle solutions
5. **Skill text is strongest lever** — The quality of the skill/workflow matters more than iteration count
6. **The Bitter Lesson** — Hand-coded heuristics always lose to learned solutions eventually

## Load Order
1. Load this `SKILL.md` (required — methodology + principles)
2. Load `genius.md` for deep patterns, hidden knowledge, and the full MetaHarness methodology
3. Load specific workflow for task
4. Cross-reference `directives/deep_self_annealing.md` for Tier 4 evolution triggers

# Self-Evolving Systems — Genius Patterns & Hidden Knowledge

> The genius of MetaHarness isn't the loop — it's what powers the loop: selective trace access, code-space regularity, and the deliberate absence of hand-coded search heuristics.

---

## Genius Patterns
### GP-1: The 6x Lever
**What it is**: Harness engineering produces a 6x performance gap on the same model weights, the same benchmark, the same task. The harness is not decoration — it IS the intelligence layer.

**How to apply**: When a workflow produces mediocre output, the instinct is to blame the model. Resist it. The workflow's prompt construction, retrieval logic, and state management are at least as responsible. Evolve those first.

**Anti-pattern**: Upgrading from Gemini 2.5 Flash to Gemini 2.5 Pro to fix a quality problem that exists in the harness.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-2: The Proposer Must Be an Agent, Not a Prompt
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-2: The Proposer Must Be an Agent, Not a Prompt
**What it is**: MetaHarness uses a coding agent (with file system access, dev tools, navigation) as its proposer — not a raw LLM with a fixed prompt. The proposer decides what to inspect, what to change, and how much to change.

**How to apply**: When running evolution loops, the proposer must have:
- Access to prior harness code (all versions, not just the best)
- Access to execution traces (actual prompts sent, actual outputs received)
- Ability to navigate and search the artifact store via grep/cat/diff
- Freedom to make local edits OR full rewrites

**Anti-pattern**: Summarizing evolution history into a fixed prompt and asking the model "what should change?" — this loses the diagnostic signal.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-3: Let It See the Failures
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-3: Let It See the Failures
**What it is**: MetaHarness imposes no parent-selection rule. The proposer can inspect ANY prior harness — including low-performing ones. This prevents local maxima by letting the proposer learn from failures, not just successes.

**How to apply**: When logging evolution history, keep ALL iterations — not just improvements. A harness that scored poorly might have one brilliant insight buried in a bad execution. The proposer can find it.

**Anti-pattern**: Only showing the proposer the top-3 performing variants.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-4: Search Set = Your Hardest Cases
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-4: Search Set = Your Hardest Cases
**What it is**: The search set should be constructed from examples the baseline gets WRONG, or a diverse subset of difficult instances. Evolution has nothing to optimize if the baseline already saturates.

**How to apply**: Mine quality gate failures, low-scoring Chain outputs, expert-standard scores < 7 as the search set. These are the cases where the current harness breaks down. Evolution targets them specifically.

**Anti-pattern**: Evaluating evolution against easy examples where everything already scores 9+.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-5: The Skill Text Dominates
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-5: The Skill Text Dominates
**What it is**: Iterating on the skill text (the instructions given to the proposer) had a larger effect on search quality than changing iteration count or population size. Run 3-5 short evolution runs specifically to debug the skill before a full run.

**How to apply**: Before running a 20-iteration evolution loop, run 3 quick 3-iteration loops focused on refining the skill/workflow description. The quality of the instructions to the proposer determines the ceiling of what evolution can discover.

**Anti-pattern**: Running 50 iterations with a mediocre skill description and expecting evolution to compensate.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-6: Code-Space Regularity Bias
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-6: Code-Space Regularity Bias
**What it is**: When harnesses are represented as programs (not templates or configs), coding models naturally propose coherent algorithms rather than brittle heuristics. Code space has an inherent regularization bias.

**How to apply**: Represent evolved artifacts as executable code or structured workflows, not arbitrary text. The proposer's coding training naturally regularizes the search toward generalizable solutions.

**Anti-pattern**: Evolving free-form prompt text where the proposer can generate arbitrary, unstructured content.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-7: Trace > Score (The Diagnostic Richness Principle)
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-7: Trace > Score (The Diagnostic Richness Principle)
**What it is**: Compressed feedback (scalar scores, summaries) removes the information needed to trace downstream failures to earlier harness decisions. Raw execution traces let the proposer form and test causal hypotheses.

**How to apply**: Log EVERYTHING: the actual prompt sent to the model, the actual response received, the state updates made, the retrieval queries issued, the files accessed. Store in JSON. Make queryable.

**Anti-pattern**: Logging only the final quality score (e.g., "7/10") without the trace that produced it.

---

chunks.section: Genius Patterns > GP-8: The Bitter Lesson Is Real
chunks.content:
## Genius Patterns
### GP-8: The Bitter Lesson Is Real
**What it is**: Rich Sutton's observation that hand-engineered heuristics always lose to learned solutions at scale. Applied to harnesses: hand-tuned prompts, manually designed workflows, and human-curated retrieval logic will be outperformed by evolved versions.

**How to apply**: Every manually-tuned component in Antigravity is a candidate for evolution. The question isn't whether to evolve it — it's when. Start with the highest-value, most-manually-tuned workflows.

**Anti-pattern**: Believing your hand-crafted workflow is already optimal because you spent a lot of time on it.

---

## Hidden Knowledge
### HK-1: The Proposer Gets Better at Proposing
**What it is**: By leaving diagnosis and edit decisions to the proposer, MetaHarness improves automatically as coding agents become more capable. Each frontier model upgrade makes all evolution loops more effective without changing anything.

**Implication**: Invest in evolution infrastructure now. It pays compound interest as models improve.

---

### HK-2: Warm-Starting from Offline Experience
**What it is**: If relevant offline experience exists (rollouts from other models, solved problem corpora, relevant papers), converting it into the same directory structure can warm-start exploration and ground new ideas.

**Implication**: Quality gate logs, past Chain finalize outputs, and session state files can all be converted into evolution warm-start material.

---

### HK-3: Lightweight Validation Saves 90% of Wasted Eval Cost
**What it is**: A simple test (import, instantiate, call on 2-3 examples) catches most malformed or nonfunctional candidates in seconds. Run this before expensive full evaluation.

**Implication**: Every evolution loop should have a fast pre-check gate. Don't spend evaluation tokens on broken candidates.

---

### HK-4: The CLI Saves Proposer Tokens
**What it is**: A small CLI that lists the Pareto frontier, shows top-k harnesses, and diffs code between runs can save the proposer significant tokens on navigation.

**Implication**: Build evolution tooling that gives the proposer shortcuts. `list-frontier`, `show-best 5`, `diff harness_003 harness_007`. This is closely aligned with how coding agents are trained.

---

### HK-5: Co-Evolution Is the Next Frontier
**What it is**: The paper's "natural next step" — co-evolve the harness AND the model weights simultaneously. The strategy shapes what the model learns, and vice versa.

**Implication**: Today we evolve harnesses around frozen models. Tomorrow we fine-tune small models with evolved harnesses, creating a double optimization loop. Watch this space.

---

## Decision Framework
Before running any evolution workflow, answer:

1. **What is the target?** — Specific workflow, prompt, retrieval logic, or orchestration pattern
2. **What is the evaluation metric?** — Quality gate score, accuracy, token cost, user satisfaction
3. **What is the search set?** — Past failures, hard examples, edge cases
4. **How many iterations?** — 5 for quick sprints, 10-20 for full evolution
5. **What is the baseline?** — Current version, documented performance
6. **What can the proposer change?** — Constraints on scope (everything? prompts only? flow only?)
7. **What is forbidden?** — Safety rails, non-negotiable behaviors, brand voice

---

## Anti-Patterns
1. **Score Worship** — Optimizing for a single number instead of understanding WHY it's that number
2. **Trace Amnesia** — Not logging execution traces, only final scores
3. **Success Bias** — Only showing the proposer winning variants, hiding failures
4. **Premature Optimization** — Running evolution on a system that hasn't been manually tuned at all yet
5. **Iteration Inflation** — Running 100 iterations when 20 would suffice (diminishing returns)
6. **Skill Neglect** — Under-investing in the skill/instruction quality for the proposer
7. **Monolithic Prompts** — Packing everything into one prompt instead of giving adaptive access

---

## Voice DNA
This skill speaks in **engineering pragmatism**:
- No hype. Results speak. "Discovered harnesses surpass hand-engineered baselines."
- Specificity over abstraction. "6x performance gap" not "significant improvement."
- Let the data lead. "Run 3-5 short cycles to debug the skill" — concrete, actionable.
- Humility about hand-engineering. "This simplicity is deliberate" — trust the system.

---

## Expert-Specific Quality Rubric
| Criterion | Score 4 (Acceptable) | Score 7 (Good) | Score 10 (Savant) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **6x Lever Application** | Identifies that harness matters, but defaults to model upgrades when quality is low. | Diagnoses whether a quality issue is model-level or harness-level, and targets the right one. | Produces a 2x+ improvement by evolving prompts, retrieval, or state management without changing model weights. |
| **Proposer Agent Quality** | Proposer is a static prompt with summarized history; loses diagnostic signal. | Proposer has trace access and can navigate prior versions, but search strategy is manual. | Proposer autonomously inspects traces, diffs prior versions, and generates targeted hypotheses with measurable predictions. |
| **Evaluation Rigor** | Uses a single score or subjective assessment; no holdout validation. | Fixed benchmark tasks with consistent rubric; detects obvious regressions. | Multi-dimensional scoring with holdout sets, statistical significance checks, and regression detection across all quality dimensions. |
| **Trace Architecture** | Logs final scores only; no execution traces or intermediate state. | Logs prompts sent and outputs received; traces are searchable but not systematically analyzed. | Full trace pipeline: prompts, outputs, timing, token counts, and per-step quality signals — all indexed and diff-able across iterations. |
| **Evolution Discipline** | Runs evolution without clear stopping criteria; iterates until budget exhausted. | Defined iteration budget with keep/discard protocol, but may over-iterate on diminishing returns. | Precise stopping criteria (convergence detection, plateau detection), binary keep/discard after each cycle, and deliberate scope constraints on what the proposer can change. |
| **Anti-Pattern Avoidance** | Falls into 2+ anti-patterns (score worship, trace amnesia, success bias) without recognizing them. | Avoids major anti-patterns but occasionally runs premature optimization or iteration inflation. | Actively monitors for all 7 anti-patterns, self-corrects when detected, and documents the correction in evolution logs. |

---

## Expert-Specific Quality Rubric
| Criterion | Score 4 (Acceptable) | Score 7 (Good) | Score 10 (Savant) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Harness-First Diagnosis** | Blames model capability for poor output without examining the workflow, prompts, or retrieval logic. | Investigates the harness before considering model upgrades, but doesn't systematically isolate the failure point. | Applies the 6x Lever principle — exhaustively diagnoses prompt construction, state management, and retrieval logic before any model-level intervention. |
| **Trace Diagnostic Richness** | Logs only final scores or pass/fail without capturing the execution trace that produced the result. | Logs prompts and outputs but misses intermediate state (retrieval queries, file access, state updates). | Captures complete execution traces in queryable format — every prompt sent, response received, state mutation, and retrieval query — enabling causal hypothesis formation. |
| **Search Set Construction** | Evaluates evolution against easy examples where the baseline already performs well. | Uses a mix of easy and hard cases, but doesn't specifically mine quality gate failures or low-scoring outputs. | Constructs the search set exclusively from the system's hardest cases — quality gate failures, expert-standard scores below 7, and edge cases where the current harness breaks down. |
| **Proposer Agency** | Summarizes evolution history into a fixed prompt and asks "what should change?" — losing diagnostic signal. | Gives the proposer access to prior versions and scores, but limits navigation and inspection capabilities. | Proposer operates as a full coding agent with file system access, grep/diff tools, access to ALL prior harnesses (including failures), and freedom to make local edits or full rewrites. |
| **Skill Text Investment** | Runs long evolution loops with mediocre skill descriptions, expecting iteration count to compensate. | Invests some effort in skill text quality but doesn't run dedicated short cycles to debug the instructions before the main evolution run. | Runs 3-5 short diagnostic cycles specifically to refine the skill/instruction text BEFORE the main evolution loop — recognizing that skill text quality determines the ceiling. |
| **Code-Space Representation** | Evolves free-form prompt text where the proposer can generate arbitrary, unstructured content. | Uses some structured format but doesn't fully leverage executable code representation for regularization. | Represents all evolved artifacts as executable code or structured workflows, exploiting coding models' natural regularization bias toward generalizable solutions. |
| **Bitter Lesson Alignment** | Treats hand-engineered workflows as sacred and resists evolution on the grounds of time invested. | Acknowledges evolution potential but only applies it to low-value or peripheral components. | Every manually-tuned component is a candidate for evolution — the question is "when," not "whether." Hand-crafted effort is respected as a warm-start, not a ceiling. |
